meta.blurb: After twelve years in Orphalese, a man waits for the ship that will take him home. Before he sails, the people ask him to speak of love, work, pain and death. Kahlil Gibran's poems have comforted readers for a century.
meta.bible: The Prophet: a book of 26 short poems in prose by Kahlil Gibran, first published in English in 1923. Kahlil Gibran: poet and painter, born in Lebanon, who lived and wrote in the United States. Almustafa: the wise man of the book, called the chosen and the beloved; he is also called the Prophet. Orphalese: the city by the sea where Almustafa has lived for twelve years. Almitra: a seeress, the first in the city to believe in him, who asks him to speak. Ielool: the month of reaping, when the ship comes. The ship: it will carry Almustafa home to the island where he was born. The people ask in turn: a rich man, an innkeeper, a ploughman, a mason, a weaver, a merchant, a judge, a lawyer, an orator, a priestess, a teacher, a youth, a scholar, an astronomer, an elder, a hermit, a poet and an old priest. The poems come in this order: Love, Marriage, Children, Giving, Eating and Drinking, Work, Joy and Sorrow, Houses, Clothes, Buying and Selling, Crime and Punishment, Laws, Freedom, Reason and Passion, Pain, Self-Knowledge, Teaching, Friendship, Talking, Time, Good and Evil, Prayer, Pleasure, Beauty, Religion, Death. Voice and tone: calm, tender, and poetic; every idea is spoken by Almustafa and attributed to him; images are of the sea, the field, the sun and the seasons. The book is respectful of all faiths and never preaches. Chapters: the book is told in twenty chapters of ten pages, from the ship in the mist to the farewell. More fixed facts: Almustafa is called the chosen and the beloved and is said to be a dawn unto his own day; the elders say he has been a noontide in their twilight; the sailors are men of his own land and sons of his ancient mother; the sea is called the sleepless mother; the temple stands in the great square; the people are called people of Orphalese; in the farewell the captain waits patiently at the helm.
chapters: The Door of Your Own Mind

beats.scene: A wise man stands on a hill above a white city by the sea
beats.summary: Introduces The Prophet, Kahlil Gibran, and Almustafa, who has waited twelve years in Orphalese for his ship.

beats.scene: A tall ship with pale sails comes slowly through the mist toward the harbour
beats.summary: On the seventh day of Ielool, Almustafa climbs a hill and sees his ship coming through the mist.

beats.scene: A man on a hilltop closes his eyes as joy rises like a bird
beats.summary: His heart opens with joy and he prays silently on the hill, before he has said a word to anyone.

beats.scene: He walks down the hill with a heavy heart and a bowed head
beats.summary: Going down the hill, a sadness comes over him, and he fears he cannot leave without a wound in the spirit.

beats.scene: Torn pieces of a heart lie scattered along the empty streets of a city
beats.summary: Pieces of his spirit lie scattered in the streets, so leaving is like tearing off a skin, yet the sea is calling and staying would freeze him.

beats.scene: A ship with sailors at its bow enters the harbour below the hill
beats.summary: At the foot of the hill he sees his ship entering the harbour and speaks to the sailors, men of his own land.

beats.scene: A river winds toward the wide sea under a pale morning sky
beats.summary: He tells the sailors and the sea he is ready; one more winding of the stream, and he will be a drop in the ocean.

beats.scene: Farmers and vine-keepers leave their work and hurry toward the city gates
beats.summary: People hurry from the fields calling his name, and he wonders what he has to give them.

beats.scene: Elders and priests crowd around him in the street, asking him to stay
beats.summary: In the city the elders and the priests beg him not to go, saying their love has never known its depth until parting.

beats.scene: A veiled woman steps from the temple into the crowded square
beats.summary: Almitra the seeress, the first to believe in him, asks him to leave them his truth before he sails.

beats.scene: Almitra asks as a hush falls over the crowd in the square
beats.summary: Almitra asks him to speak of love; a stillness falls and he tells them to follow love when it calls, though its ways are hard and steep.

beats.scene: Great wings fold around a traveller on a steep stony path
beats.summary: Yield when love's wings enfold you, though a hidden sword may wound; believe his voice, though it shatters your dreams.

beats.scene: A gardener prunes a tree whose branches glow in the morning sun
beats.summary: Love crowns you and wounds you, helps you grow and prunes you, lifts you to the sun and shakes your roots.

beats.scene: Golden sheaves of corn are gathered, ground and baked into bread
beats.summary: Love gathers us like sheaves of corn, threshes, sifts, grinds and kneads us, then bakes us as sacred bread.

beats.scene: A person kneels in a still field with both hands on a glowing heart
beats.summary: Love does all this so that we learn the secrets of our own hearts and become a fragment of Life's heart.

beats.scene: A person leaves a threshing floor and walks into a grey seasonless land
beats.summary: If you seek only love's peace and pleasure, leave the threshing floor for a world with no seasons, where you laugh and weep only a little.

beats.scene: A single flame burns alone in a bowl, needing nothing else
beats.summary: Love gives nothing but itself and takes only from itself; it does not own and cannot be owned, for love is enough for love.

beats.scene: A traveller walks a bright road, drawn forward by a glowing hand
beats.summary: Do not say God is in my heart but I am in the heart of God; you cannot direct love, it directs you if it finds you worthy.

beats.scene: A brook runs over stones in moonlight and sings to the night
beats.summary: Love wants only to fulfil itself; if you must have desires, let them be to melt like a brook, to know the pain of tenderness, and to bleed willingly.

beats.scene: A person wakes at dawn, rests at noon and comes home at dusk
beats.summary: A lover's day: wake at dawn with a winged heart, rest at noon, return home with gratitude, and sleep with a prayer for the beloved.

beats.scene: Almitra and a young couple stand close together in the crowd
beats.summary: Almitra asks about marriage while a young bride and groom hold hands tightly in the crowd.

beats.scene: Two figures walk together over a hill under a wide evening sky
beats.summary: You were born together and will be together always, even when death's white wings scatter your days, even in God's silent memory.

beats.scene: Two people stand apart on a hill while bright wind passes between
beats.summary: But there must be spaces in your togetherness, so that the winds of heaven can dance between you.

beats.scene: A moving blue sea lies between two quiet shores at dusk
beats.summary: Love one another, but do not make love a bond; let it be a moving sea between the shores of your souls.

beats.scene: Two cups of wine and two loaves on a table between a couple
beats.summary: Fill each other's cup but drink from separate ones; give each other bread but do not eat from the same loaf.

beats.scene: A lute lies between two dancers as their joyful feet circle it
beats.summary: Sing and dance together and be joyful, but let each be alone, like the strings of a lute that quiver with the same music.

beats.scene: Two open hands each hold a small glowing heart
beats.summary: Give your hearts, but not into each other's keeping, for only the hand of Life can hold your hearts.

beats.scene: Two temple pillars stand apart, with an oak and a cypress beside them
beats.summary: Stand together, yet not too near: the temple's pillars stand apart, and the oak and the cypress do not grow in each other's shadow.

beats.scene: A young bride and groom loosen their hands and smile at each other
beats.summary: In the crowd, the young couple loosen their grip and smile, for they see that room between them is not distance.

beats.scene: A mother with a baby presses through the crowd toward the speaker
beats.summary: A woman holding a baby presses through the crowd, and the people make room for her to ask her question.

beats.scene: A mother holds her baby close and asks her question
beats.summary: The woman asks him to speak of children, and he says her children are not hers, but the sons and daughters of Life's longing for itself.

beats.scene: Light passes through a window into a quiet room where a child plays
beats.summary: They come through you but not from you; though they are with you, they do not belong to you.

beats.scene: A child talks eagerly while a parent listens with a gentle smile
beats.summary: You may give your children your love but not your thoughts, for they have thoughts of their own.

beats.scene: A small house stands in sunlight beside a distant house of dawn
beats.summary: You may house their bodies but not their souls, for their souls live in the house of tomorrow, which you cannot visit even in dreams.

beats.scene: A parent and child stand side by side, both facing forward on a road
beats.summary: You may strive to be like them but not make them like you, for life does not go backward or linger with yesterday.

beats.scene: A baby grips its mother's finger and gazes up at the speaker
beats.summary: The baby in the woman's arms wakes and grips her finger; Almustafa smiles at the child and the crowd falls quiet.

beats.scene: An archer stands with a drawn bow beside a row of arrows
beats.summary: You are the bows and your children are living arrows; the Archer sees the mark on the path of the infinite.

beats.scene: The bow bends under the strong hands of an unseen archer
beats.summary: The Archer bends you with His might so that His arrows may go swift and far.

beats.scene: An arrow flies toward the horizon over a field of golden grass
beats.summary: Let your bending in the Archer's hand be for gladness, for He loves the arrow that flies and also the bow that is steady.

beats.scene: A father lifts his small son onto his shoulders to see the sea
beats.summary: A father in the crowd lifts his son to see the ship; the mother kisses her baby and thanks him, and a rich man stirs to speak.

beats.scene: A rich man in fine clothes asks his question beside glinting coins
beats.summary: The rich man asks about giving; Almustafa says you give little when you give your things and truly give when you give yourself.

beats.scene: A small dog buries bones in the sand while pilgrims walk away
beats.summary: The over-careful dog burying bones in the trackless sand shows that fear of need is itself a need.

beats.scene: A heavy coin purse lies beside a poor woman sharing her only loaf
beats.summary: Some give a little of the much they own and want to be noticed; others have little and give it all, trusting life.

beats.scene: A myrtle bush scatters sweet air across a quiet green valley
beats.summary: Some give with joy, some with pain, and some like the myrtle that breathes its fragrance into the valley, and through them God speaks.

beats.scene: Orchard trees heavy with fruit bend over a flock grazing below
beats.summary: It is well to give when asked but better to give unasked; give now, for the trees and flocks do not give only to the deserving.

beats.scene: The rich man lowers his eyes as warm light spills across the square
beats.summary: Who are you that people should unveil their pride before you give? See that you deserve to give; it is Life that gives to Life, and you are only a witness.

beats.scene: An old innkeeper sets a table with fruit, bread and wine
beats.summary: The old innkeeper asks about eating and drinking; Almustafa says he wishes people could live on the earth's fragrance, but since they must take life to eat, let it be an act of worship.

beats.scene: A simple table glows like an altar with fruit and bread laid upon it
beats.summary: Let your table be an altar on which the gifts of forest and plain are offered for that which is purer in you.

beats.scene: A hand holds a red apple with green leaves in morning light
beats.summary: Say to the creature you take that the same law will take you; and say to the apple that its seeds will live in your body.

beats.scene: Purple grapes are pressed in autumn and red wine is poured in winter
beats.summary: In autumn, when you gather grapes, say you too are a vineyard; in winter, when you pour wine, let a song be in your heart for each cup.

beats.scene: A ploughman steps from the crowd with mud on his boots
beats.summary: A ploughman asks about work; Almustafa says we work to keep pace with the earth, for to be idle is to become a stranger to the seasons.

beats.scene: A reed flute sounds in a field as the hours turn to music
beats.summary: When you work you are a flute through whose heart the whispering of the hours turns to music; who would be a silent reed when all else sings?

beats.scene: A tired worker pauses in a field as the sun lights the earth
beats.summary: You have been told work is a curse; but in working you fulfil a part of the earth's dream, and to love life through labour is to know its inmost secret.

beats.scene: A lantern is lit in a dark field and a hand reaches to it
beats.summary: Life is dark without urge, urge is blind without knowledge, knowledge is vain without work, and work is empty without love.

beats.scene: A weaver at her loom holds up cloth, thinking of someone dear
beats.summary: To work with love is to weave as if your beloved will wear the cloth, build as if your beloved will live there, and sow as if your beloved will eat.

beats.scene: A carver shapes a block of wood while shadowy figures stand around him
beats.summary: Fill everything you make with a breath of your own spirit, and know that all the blessed dead stand about you, watching.

beats.scene: A sculptor and a ploughman glance at each other, each proud of his craft
beats.summary: People say the carver of marble is nobler than the ploughman; but the wind speaks no more sweetly to the oak than to a blade of grass.

beats.scene: A figure at the temple gate holds out a bowl while workers sing
beats.summary: Work is love made visible; if you can work only with distaste, sit at the temple gate and take alms from those who work with joy.

beats.scene: A baker pulls a bitter loaf from the oven, shaking his head
beats.summary: If you bake bread with indifference it is bitter and feeds only half of man's hunger; a grudge puts poison in the wine.

beats.scene: A weaver and a baker stand together, listening to a song
beats.summary: Even if you sing like an angel, without love you muffle the voices of the day and the night; the baker and the weaver listen.

beats.scene: A woman sits holding a cup and wiping a tear
beats.summary: A woman asks about joy and sorrow; Almustafa says joy is sorrow unmasked, and the well from which laughter rises was often filled with tears.

beats.scene: A potter lifts a glowing cup from his oven beside a hollowed lute
beats.summary: The deeper sorrow carves into you, the more joy you can hold; the cup that holds wine was burned in the oven, the lute hollowed with knives.

beats.scene: A man looks into his own heart, glowing like a lit window
beats.summary: When you are joyful, look deep in your heart: what gave you sorrow now gives you joy; when sorrowful, you weep for what once delighted you.

beats.scene: Two people at a table argue while a third sleeps on the bed behind
beats.summary: Some say joy is greater, others sorrow; they are inseparable, and when one sits alone with you at table, the other is asleep on your bed.

beats.scene: A pair of golden scales hangs level in a treasure-keeper's quiet hand
beats.summary: You are suspended like scales between joy and sorrow; only when you are empty are you still and balanced.

beats.scene: A mason with dusty hands steps forward beside a simple tent
beats.summary: A mason asks about houses; Almustafa says to build a bower in the wilderness before building a house within the city walls.

beats.scene: A sleeping house in moonlight dreams of green hills and open meadows
beats.summary: Your house is your larger body, growing in the sun and sleeping at night; does it not dream of leaving the city for the grove or hilltop?

beats.scene: A heavy locked door stands in a high wall beside a stone house
beats.summary: He asks what they keep in their houses behind fastened doors: peace, memories, beauty, or only comfort.

beats.scene: A silk-gloved hand rests on a chair as a guest becomes the master
beats.summary: Comfort enters as a guest, becomes the host, then the master; its hands are silken but its heart is iron, and it kills the soul's passion.

beats.scene: A tall mast rises from a small house into the open sky
beats.summary: But you shall not be trapped or tamed; your house shall be a mast, not an anchor, an eyelid that guards the eye, and your longing dwells in the mansion of the sky.

beats.scene: A weaver holds up a bright robe in the afternoon light
beats.summary: A weaver asks about clothes; Almustafa says clothes conceal much of our beauty but hide nothing of the unbeautiful, and can become a harness and a chain.

beats.scene: Sunlight and wind touch a person with bare arms on a hillside
beats.summary: He wishes people could meet the sun and wind with more skin and less clothing, for the breath of life is in sunlight and its hand is in the wind.

beats.scene: A cold north wind weaves threads on a great loom in a forest
beats.summary: Some say the north wind wove our clothes; yes, but shame was his loom and the softening of the sinews his thread; when his work was done he laughed in the forest.

beats.scene: A shield of polished metal reflects a fearful face in the crowd
beats.summary: Modesty is a shield against the eye of the unclean; when the unclean are no more, modesty would be a fetter and a fouling of the mind.

beats.scene: A barefoot child runs through grass with the wind in her hair
beats.summary: The earth delights to feel your bare feet and the winds long to play with your hair; a child who was scolded for running barefoot is set free.

beats.scene: A merchant weighs fruit and cloth at a busy market stall
beats.summary: A merchant asks about buying and selling; Almustafa says the earth yields her fruit, and in exchanging her gifts you find abundance.

beats.scene: Two traders hold a scale with one side heaped with grain
beats.summary: Unless exchange is made in love and kindly justice, it will lead some to greed and others to hunger.

beats.scene: Buyers and sellers meet among stalls of fish, cloth, pots and spices
beats.summary: In the market place, call on the master spirit of the earth to bless the scales; do not let those who only sell words take part, but send them to the field or the sea.

beats.scene: Singers, dancers and a flute player arrive at the busy market
beats.summary: If singers, dancers and flute players come, buy their gifts too, for they gather fruit and frankincense, and their dreams are food for the soul.

beats.scene: A merchant stands thoughtfully by his scales as the market closes at dusk
beats.summary: Before leaving the market place, see that no one goes away empty-handed, for the master spirit of the earth will not sleep until the needs of the least of you are met.

beats.scene: An old judge in a long robe steps forward from the crowd
beats.summary: A judge asks about crime and punishment; Almustafa says wrong is done when the spirit wanders unguarded, and a wrong against others is a wrong against oneself.

beats.scene: A calm ocean and rising sun above a figure walking asleep in mist
beats.summary: Your god-self is like the ocean and the sun, undefiled; but much in you is still man, and much is not yet man, a shapeless sleeper in the mist.

beats.scene: A crowd points at one lonely figure while a mirror shows the same face
beats.summary: You speak of a wrongdoer as a stranger; but as the holy cannot rise above the highest in you, the wicked cannot fall below the lowest in you.

beats.scene: One yellow leaf hangs on a green tree while a procession walks below
beats.summary: A single leaf turns yellow only with the silent knowledge of the whole tree; you walk as a procession, and when one falls he falls for those behind and ahead.

beats.scene: A heavy stone lies in a road while a crowd walks around it
beats.summary: He admits his words are heavy: the wronged and the righteous are not wholly apart from the world's wrongs, and the condemned often carries the burden of the guiltless.

beats.scene: A black thread and a white thread are woven together on a loom
beats.summary: You cannot separate the just from the unjust; they are woven together like black and white threads, and when the black thread breaks the weaver must examine the whole cloth and the loom.

beats.scene: A woodcutter with an axe studies the deep roots of a tree
beats.summary: Before judging, weigh the heart of the other person too; and if you would lay the axe to the evil tree, look to its roots, where good and bad are entwined.

beats.scene: A row of judges sits silently, one with a hand on his chin
beats.summary: He asks the judges what penalty fits a man honest in deed but a thief in spirit, or one who deceives yet has himself been wronged.

beats.scene: A man sits alone at night with his face in his hands
beats.summary: How shall you punish those whose remorse is already greater than their wrong? Remorse is the justice of the very law you serve, and it cannot be laid on the innocent or lifted from the guilty.

beats.scene: A fallen man and a standing man are one figure in twilight
beats.summary: To understand justice, look at every deed in the fullness of light; the erect and the fallen are one man in twilight, and the old judge bows his head.

beats.scene: Children build sand towers by the sea as a wave rolls in
beats.summary: A lawyer asks about laws; Almustafa says people love making laws but love breaking them more, like children who build sand towers and knock them down.

beats.scene: A wave laughs over sand towers while children shout and clap
beats.summary: While you build sand towers the ocean brings more sand, and when you destroy them the ocean laughs with you, for it always laughs with the innocent.

beats.scene: A man chisels a great rock into a stern figure in his own image
beats.summary: But what of those to whom life is a rock and law a chisel with which they carve it in their own likeness?

beats.scene: A man stands in bright sunlight with his back turned to the sun
beats.summary: These people stand in the sunlight but with their backs to the sun; they see only their shadows, and their shadows are their laws.

beats.scene: A skylark rises singing over a muffled drum and a loosened lyre
beats.summary: No image drawn on the earth can hold those who walk facing the sun; you can muffle the drum and loosen the lyre, but who can command the skylark not to sing?

beats.scene: An orator steps from the crowd, one hand raised, at the city gate
beats.summary: An orator asks about freedom; Almustafa says he has seen people bow and worship their own freedom, as slaves praise a tyrant who destroys them.

beats.scene: A free man in fine clothes wears a heavy yoke around his neck
beats.summary: You are free only when even the search for freedom becomes a harness, and you stop speaking of freedom as a goal.

beats.scene: A person rises above a dark cloud of cares into bright morning air
beats.summary: You are free when your days have cares and your nights have wants and griefs, yet you rise above them; for that you must break the chains you made yourself.

beats.scene: A glittering chain with bright links hangs around a proud neck
beats.summary: What you call freedom is the strongest chain, though its links glitter; the unjust law you would abolish was written by your own hand, and the tyrant must be dethroned within you first.

beats.scene: Light and shadow dance in pairs on a bright wall as chains fall
beats.summary: The care you wish to cast off you chose, and the seat of fear is in your heart; light and shadow cling in pairs, and a freedom without fetters becomes the fetter of a greater freedom.

beats.scene: A priestess in a white robe addresses the crowd beneath gathering clouds
beats.summary: The priestess asks about reason and passion; Almustafa says the soul is often a battlefield on which reason and judgment fight passion and appetite.

beats.scene: A peacemaker stands between two groups with open, outstretched hands
beats.summary: He wishes he could be the peacemaker in their souls, but he cannot unless they themselves become the lovers of all their elements.

beats.scene: A small boat on a stormy sea with a rudder and white sails
beats.summary: Reason and passion are the rudder and sails of your seafaring soul; if either is broken you toss and drift or stand still in mid-sea.

beats.scene: A great stone wall stands beside a wild bonfire that burns itself out
beats.summary: Reason ruling alone is a confining force, and passion unattended is a flame that burns to its own destruction.

beats.scene: A bird made of fire rises from grey ashes into a bright sky
beats.summary: Let your soul lift reason to the height of passion so it can sing, and guide passion with reason so it rises each day like the phoenix from its ashes.

beats.scene: Two guests sit at a table, each served the same bread and wine
beats.summary: Treat your judgment and your appetite as two loved guests; you would not honour one above the other, for whoever favours one loses the love and trust of both.

beats.scene: White poplars shade a green meadow where a person sits at peace
beats.summary: Among the hills, in the shade of white poplars, let your heart say in silence that God rests in reason.

beats.scene: Lightning splits a dark sky above a forest shaken by great wind
beats.summary: When the storm comes and thunder and lightning proclaim the majesty of the sky, let your heart say in awe that God moves in passion.

beats.scene: A single green leaf trembles on a vast tree in a great forest
beats.summary: Since you are a breath in God's sphere and a leaf in God's forest, you too should rest in reason and move in passion.

beats.scene: His ship in the harbour tugs at its anchor with sails and rudder ready
beats.summary: Out in the harbour his ship tugs at its anchor with sails and rudder in balance; the people turn, and a woman steps forward to ask about pain.

beats.scene: A woman with a sorrowful face stands with her hands folded
beats.summary: The woman asks about pain; Almustafa says pain is the breaking of the shell that encloses your understanding.

beats.scene: A fruit stone cracks open to let its heart into sunlight
beats.summary: As the stone of the fruit must break so that its heart may stand in the sun, so you must know pain.

beats.scene: Rain, snow and spring flowers pass over the same quiet field
beats.summary: If you could keep your heart in wonder at the daily miracles of life, your pain would seem as wondrous as your joy, and you would accept the seasons of your heart.

beats.scene: A hand pours a dark medicine into a cup in a quiet room
beats.summary: Much of your pain is self-chosen; it is the bitter potion by which the physician within you heals your sick self, so trust him and drink the remedy in silence.

beats.scene: Two gentle hands hold a clay cup, one rough and one tender
beats.summary: The physician's hand, though heavy and hard, is guided by the tender hand of the Unseen, and his cup is made of clay the Potter moistened with His own sacred tears.

beats.scene: A man sits alone beside a still lake at dawn
beats.summary: A man asks about self-knowledge; Almustafa says your hearts know in silence the secrets of the days and nights, but your ears thirst for the sound of that knowledge.

beats.scene: A hidden spring bubbles from a hillside and runs toward the sea
beats.summary: It is well that you should seek to know; the hidden wellspring of your soul must rise and run murmuring to the sea, and its treasure will be revealed.

beats.scene: A staff and a coil of rope lie unused beside a deep dark lake
beats.summary: Let there be no scales to weigh your treasure, and do not search your depths with a staff or a sounding line, for the self is a sea, boundless and measureless.

beats.scene: A traveller on a path meets a glowing figure walking toward him
beats.summary: Do not say I have found the truth but I have found a truth; do not say I have found the path of the soul but I have met the soul walking upon my path.

beats.scene: A lotus with countless petals opens slowly on still water
beats.summary: The soul walks upon all paths; it does not walk on a line nor grow like a reed; it unfolds itself like a lotus of countless petals.

beats.scene: A teacher stands at a temple door among his students
beats.summary: A teacher asks about teaching; Almustafa says no one can reveal to you anything except what already lies half asleep in the dawning of your knowledge.

beats.scene: A teacher points his students toward a quiet open doorway
beats.summary: The teacher who walks in the shadow of the temple gives not his wisdom but his faith and lovingness; if he is wise he leads you to the threshold of your own mind.

beats.scene: A starry sky above a musician with a harp and an astronomer
beats.summary: The astronomer can tell you his understanding of space but cannot give it to you; the musician can sing the rhythm of space but cannot give you the ear that catches it.

beats.scene: A mathematician with a slate points toward a far distant country
beats.summary: Whoever is learned in numbers can tell of weight and measure but cannot lead you there; the vision of one man lends not its wings to another.

beats.scene: Many separate figures stand alone under one wide starry sky
beats.summary: Each of you stands alone in God's knowledge, so each must be alone in his knowledge of God and understanding of the earth; the teacher nods and lowers his lamp.

beats.scene: A youth with bright eyes steps forward from a group of friends
beats.summary: A youth asks about friendship; Almustafa says your friend is your needs answered, the field you sow with love and reap with thanks.

beats.scene: Two friends sit quietly together by a warm fire
beats.summary: When your friend speaks his mind you fear not your own no or withhold your yes; when he is silent your heart keeps listening to his heart.

beats.scene: A climber looks back at a mountain that is clearer from the plain
beats.summary: When you part from your friend you do not grieve, for what you love most in him may be clearer in his absence, as a mountain is clearer to the climber from the plain.

beats.scene: A fisherman's empty net lies tangled on a quiet shore
beats.summary: Let there be no purpose in friendship except the deepening of the spirit; love that seeks anything else is a net cast forth, and only the unprofitable is caught.

beats.scene: Friends laugh together at dawn with dew shining on the grass
beats.summary: Let your best be for your friend; seek him always with hours to live; and in the sweetness of friendship let there be laughter, for in the dew of little things the heart finds its morning.

beats.scene: A scholar with an armful of scrolls stands among the crowd
beats.summary: A scholar asks about talking; Almustafa says you talk when you cease to be at peace with your thoughts, and then sound becomes a pastime.

beats.scene: A small bird beats its wings inside a narrow cage of words
beats.summary: In much of your talking, thinking is half murdered; a thought in a cage of words may unfold its wings but cannot fly.

beats.scene: A man chatters loudly to a crowd to avoid an empty silent room
beats.summary: Some seek the talkative through fear of being alone, because the silence of aloneness shows them their naked selves; others reveal a truth they do not understand.

beats.scene: An old woman sits silently in a quiet garden, her face at peace
beats.summary: Some have the truth within them but do not tell it in words; in their hearts the spirit dwells in rhythmic silence.

beats.scene: Two friends meet on a sunlit road with a vineyard behind them
beats.summary: When you meet your friend let the spirit in you move your lips; let the voice within your voice speak to the ear of his ear, and his soul will keep the truth of your heart.

beats.scene: An astronomer holds a watch and a sundial under a starry sky
beats.summary: An astronomer asks about time; Almustafa says you would measure the measureless and make time a stream upon whose bank you sit to watch it flow.

beats.scene: A sunrise and a sunset glow together in one wide sky
beats.summary: Yet the timeless in you knows life's timelessness, and knows that yesterday is only today's memory and tomorrow is today's dream.

beats.scene: Scattering stars burst from one bright point into a dark sky
beats.summary: That which sings and contemplates in you still dwells within the first moment that scattered the stars into space.

beats.scene: A heart glows like a small sun at the centre of a person
beats.summary: Who does not feel his power to love is boundless, yet dwelling at the centre of his being, moving not from thought to thought? Time, like love, is undivided and paceless.

beats.scene: Four seasons circle one another around a single glowing sun
beats.summary: If in thought you must measure time into seasons, let each season encircle all the others; let today embrace the past with remembrance and the future with longing.

beats.scene: An elder of the city in a grey cloak speaks from the front
beats.summary: An elder asks about good and evil; Almustafa says he can speak of the good in them but not of the evil, for evil is only good tortured by its own hunger and thirst.

beats.scene: A hungry traveller drinks from a dark cave pool in the night
beats.summary: When good is hungry it seeks food even in dark caves, and when it thirsts it drinks even of dead waters.

beats.scene: A divided house with two doors stands beside a drifting ship
beats.summary: You are good when you are one with yourself, but when you are not you are not evil; a divided house is only a divided house, and a ship without a rudder may wander but not sink.

beats.scene: A tree root clings to dark earth below a fruit-laden branch
beats.summary: You are good when you strive to give of yourself, but not evil when you seek gain, for then you are a root clinging to the earth; the fruit cannot ask the root to be like it.

beats.scene: Ripe fruit hangs in the sun while its roots drink in the dark
beats.summary: To the fruit giving is a need, as receiving is a need to the root; each is good in its own place.

beats.scene: A sleepy man mumbles clumsy words while a child listens kindly
beats.summary: You are good when fully awake in your speech, but not evil when you sleep while your tongue staggers; even stumbling speech may strengthen a weak tongue.

beats.scene: A strong walker slows his pace to match a limping friend
beats.summary: You are good when you walk with bold steps, yet not evil when you limp; even those who limp do not go backward, but the strong must not limp before the lame, deeming it kindness.

beats.scene: A stag and a turtle stand side by side on a forest road
beats.summary: You are good in countless ways, and you are not evil when you are not good, but only loitering and sluggish; stags cannot teach swiftness to turtles.

beats.scene: A torrent rushes to the sea beside a flat stream winding slowly
beats.summary: In your longing for your giant self lies your goodness; in some it is a torrent rushing to the sea, in others a flat stream that lingers in bends.

beats.scene: A traveller offers his cloak to a barefoot stranger without asking questions
beats.summary: Let not him who longs much scold him who longs little; the truly good ask not the naked where their garment is, nor the houseless about their house; the elder bows his head.

beats.scene: A priestess kneels in a quiet temple as light pours through its windows
beats.summary: A priestess asks about prayer; Almustafa says you pray in distress and need, and wishes you would pray also in the fullness of your joy.

beats.scene: A person opens both arms toward the sky at sunrise
beats.summary: What is prayer but the expansion of yourself into the living air? If it comforts you to pour out your darkness, it is also a joy to pour out the dawning of your heart.

beats.scene: Distant figures rise toward a bright temple made only of air
beats.summary: When you pray you rise to meet those who are praying at that very hour; enter the invisible temple for joy and communion, not only to ask.

beats.scene: A priestess listens as wind, sea and mountains murmur a prayer
beats.summary: He cannot teach prayer in words, for God hears words only when He speaks them through our lips; but those born of the mountains, forests and seas can find their prayer in the heart.

beats.scene: A quiet night sky above sleeping mountains, forests and the sea
beats.summary: In the stillness of the night they pray: our God, who art our winged self, thy will in us wills; thou art our need, and in giving us more of thyself thou givest us all.

beats.scene: A hermit in a plain robe walks down from the hills
beats.summary: A hermit who visits the city once a year asks about pleasure; Almustafa says pleasure is a freedom-song but not freedom itself, the blossoming of desires but not their fruit.

beats.scene: Young people laugh and dance while an elder frowns at them
beats.summary: Some of your youth seek pleasure as if it were all and are rebuked; he would let them seek, for in seeking they will find pleasure and her seven sisters, each more beautiful than pleasure.

beats.scene: A digger finds a chest of gold while searching for roots
beats.summary: A man who dug for roots found a treasure; elders remember pleasures with regret, but should remember them with gratitude, like a summer's harvest.

beats.scene: A nightingale sings under stars as a firefly glows beside it
beats.summary: Some shun every pleasure for fear of offending the spirit; but who can offend the spirit? Your body is the harp of your soul.

beats.scene: A bee gathers honey from a flower in a sunlit garden
beats.summary: The bee loves to take honey and the flower loves to give it; to both the giving and receiving of pleasure is a need and an ecstasy. Be like the flowers and the bees.

beats.scene: A poet with an open notebook stands at the edge of the crowd
beats.summary: A poet asks about beauty; Almustafa says you cannot find beauty unless she herself is your way and guide, nor speak of her unless she weaves your speech.

beats.scene: A shy young mother walks quietly among a gentle crowd
beats.summary: The aggrieved and the injured say that beauty is kind and gentle, like a young mother half shy of her own glory.

beats.scene: A great storm shakes the mountains while a woman with wild hair watches
beats.summary: The passionate say that beauty is a thing of might and dread, like the tempest that shakes the earth beneath us and the sky above us.

beats.scene: A tired traveller listens to a quiet voice as a candle flickers
beats.summary: The tired say beauty speaks in soft whispers, like a faint light that quivers in fear of the shadow; the restless say they have heard her shouting among the mountains.

beats.scene: A night watchman and a tired farmer look to the east and the west
beats.summary: At night the watchmen say beauty will rise with the dawn from the east, and at noon the wayfarers say they have seen her leaning from the windows of the sunset.

beats.scene: Snow-bound villagers and sweating reapers each point to a different season
beats.summary: In winter the snow-bound say she will come with the spring, leaping on the hills; in summer the reapers say they saw her dancing with the autumn leaves, with snow in her hair.

beats.scene: A crowd of open hands reaches toward an empty horizon
beats.summary: All these things you have said of beauty, yet you spoke not of her but of needs unsatisfied; and beauty is not a need but an ecstasy.

beats.scene: A smiling person with closed eyes sees a glowing garden within
beats.summary: Beauty is not a thirsty mouth or an empty hand, but an enflamed heart and an enchanted soul; an image you see with closed eyes and a song you hear with covered ears.

beats.scene: A flower garden in bloom beside a flock of white birds in flight
beats.summary: Beauty is not the sap within the furrowed bark nor a wing attached to a claw, but a garden for ever in bloom and a flock of angels for ever in flight.

beats.scene: A veil lifts from a holy face reflected in a great mirror
beats.summary: Beauty is life when life unveils her holy face, but you are life and you are the veil; beauty is eternity gazing at itself in a mirror, and you are the mirror.

beats.scene: An old priest in a white robe stands before the temple door
beats.summary: An old priest asks about religion; Almustafa asks whether he has spoken of anything else today, for religion is all deeds and reflection, and a wonder ever springing in the soul.

beats.scene: A stonecutter and a weaver work beside a spilling hourglass
beats.summary: Who can separate faith from actions, or belief from occupations? Who can spread his hours out and say, this for God and this for myself?

beats.scene: Hours like winged birds fly across the sky from one person to another
beats.summary: All your hours are wings that beat through space from self to self; whoever wears his morality as his best garment would be better naked.

beats.scene: A songbird sings in a cage while an open window shows the sky
beats.summary: Whoever defines his conduct by ethics alone imprisons his songbird in a cage; the freest song never comes through bars and wires.

beats.scene: A window opens and shuts beside a house with windows of dawn
beats.summary: He to whom worship is a window to open and shut has not yet visited the house of his soul, whose windows stand open from dawn to dawn.

beats.scene: A farmer, a smith and a musician carry their tools into a temple
beats.summary: Your daily life is your temple and your religion; whenever you enter it take with you your all, the plough, the forge, the mallet and the lute.

beats.scene: People of every kind walk together into a great temple
beats.summary: In reverie you cannot rise above your achievements nor fall below your failures; take all people with you, for in adoration you cannot fly higher than their hopes.

beats.scene: A child plays in the doorway of a temple, laughing and clapping
beats.summary: If you would know God, do not be a solver of riddles; look around you and you will see Him playing with your children.

beats.scene: A great cloud drifts over mountains as lightning and rain fall
beats.summary: Look into space; you will see Him walking in the cloud, stretching out His arms in the lightning and coming down in rain.

beats.scene: A flowering bush and a tall tree wave in a gentle breeze
beats.summary: You shall see Him smiling in flowers, then rising and waving His hands in trees; the old priest bows and looks at the world as if for the first time.

beats.scene: Almitra stands among the silent crowd in the dusk
beats.summary: Almitra steps forward and asks Almustafa to speak to the people about death.

beats.scene: Almustafa looks gently at Almitra as stillness settles on the square
beats.summary: Almustafa answers that they wish to know the secret of death.

beats.scene: Almustafa points toward a garden full of leaves, birds and children
beats.summary: He says they can only find the secret by looking for it in the heart of life.

beats.scene: An owl sits in a dark tree at noon beside a river
beats.summary: The owl, whose night-bound eyes are blind in the day, cannot unveil the mystery of light.

beats.scene: Almustafa opens his arms wide toward leaves, birds, flowing water and children
beats.summary: If they wish to see the spirit of death, they must open the heart wide to the body of life.

beats.scene: A river runs through a green valley and meets the open sea
beats.summary: Life and death are one, even as the river and the sea are one.

beats.scene: A man sits by a window at night and gazes toward the far stars
beats.summary: In the depth of their hopes and desires lies their silent knowledge of the beyond.

beats.scene: Seeds sleep under deep snow in a quiet field
beats.summary: Like seeds dreaming under the snow, the heart dreams of spring; in those dreams hides the gate to eternity.

beats.scene: A shepherd trembles before a king who raises a hand to honour him
beats.summary: Fear of death is the trembling of a shepherd before a king whose hand will be laid on him in honour.

beats.scene: A figure stands alone on a hilltop with the wind in his robe
beats.summary: To die is to stand naked in the wind and melt into the sun.

beats.scene: A man breathes freely on a hilltop under a wide open sky
beats.summary: To cease breathing is to free the breath from its restless tides, so that it may rise and seek God unburdened.

beats.scene: A silent river flows through a still valley under a pale moon
beats.summary: Only when they drink from the river of silence will they truly sing.

beats.scene: A traveller reaches a high mountain top and begins to dance on the rocks
beats.summary: When they reach the mountain top they will begin to climb, and when the earth claims their limbs they will truly dance.

beats.scene: Evening falls on the temple as lamps are lit across the great square
beats.summary: Evening comes; Almitra blesses the day, the place and the spirit that spoke, and Almustafa wonders whether he was also a listener.

beats.scene: The crowd follows Almustafa down the temple steps toward the harbour
beats.summary: Almustafa goes down the steps of the temple, the people follow, and he steps aboard his ship.

beats.scene: Almustafa stands on the ship's deck facing the crowd on the shore
beats.summary: From the deck he tells the people the wind bids him go; wanderers never begin a day where they ended the last.

beats.scene: A coiled rope lies on the deck as the light fades over the crowd
beats.summary: His days among them were brief and his words briefer; if his voice fades, he will return with a richer heart.

beats.scene: Sailors wait by the ropes while the captain looks toward the open sea
beats.summary: He tells the sailors that they sailed in his dreams and will now sail in his awakening, and that he is ready.

beats.scene: Almustafa raises one hand in farewell to the crowd on the shore
beats.summary: He tells them their meeting was a dream that is over; if they meet again in memory they will sing a deeper song.

beats.scene: The ship sails east into the mist as a woman watches
beats.summary: The ship sails; Almitra, alone on the sea wall, remembers his promise that another woman shall bear him.

A1A2: Almustafa lived in the city of Orphalese for twelve long years.
One morning he climbed a hill and saw his ship in the mist.
His heart was full of joy, and he closed his eyes to pray.
Walking down, he felt sad, because leaving would not be easy.
He had left pieces of his heart in every street.
At the bottom of the hill, he saw sailors from his own land.
He told the great sea that he was ready to come.
People left their fields and ran to the city gates.
The elders asked him not to leave them yet.
Almitra, a wise woman, asked him to share his truth.
Almitra asked, “Please tell us about love,” and everyone became quiet.
Love has wings that may hurt you, but you must trust them.
Love helps you grow, and sometimes it hurts you too.
Love takes us like corn and makes us into bread.
Love does this so we can know our own hearts.
If you want only easy love, your laughing and crying will be small.
Love gives only itself, and it takes only from itself.
Do not try to lead love, because love will lead you.
Be like a stream that sings its song to the night.
At dawn, thank the day, and at night, pray for the one you love.
Then Almitra asked, “What can you tell us about marriage, master?”
You were born together, and you will be together always.
But leave some space between you, so the wind can come through.
Love each other, but do not tie each other down.
Fill each other's cup, but drink from your own cup.
Sing and dance together, but also be alone sometimes.
Give your heart, but do not give it to keep.
The pillars of a temple stand apart from each other.
The young pair let go of their hands and smiled.
A woman with a baby came forward from the crowd.
The woman said, “Please tell us about children.”
Children come through you, but they do not belong to you.
Give them your love, but let them think their own thoughts.
You can give them a house, but their souls live in tomorrow.
Life does not go backward, so let your child be different.
The baby woke up and held its mother's finger.
You are the bow, and your children are living arrows.
The Archer bends the bow, and the arrow flies far.
Be glad in the Archer's hand, for He loves you too.
A father lifted his son so the boy could see the ship.
Real giving is giving yourself, not only your things.
A dog hid his bones in the sand for tomorrow.
Some people give a little and want everyone to see.
A flower gives its sweet smell to the whole valley.
Give now, and do not wait until you are asked.
It is really life that gives to life.
A man from the inn asked how people should eat and drink.
Treat your table like a holy place, and be thankful.
When you eat an apple, thank it in your heart.
In winter, sing a little song for each cup of wine.
We work to keep pace with the earth, he said.
When you work, you are like a flute that makes music.
Some say work is a curse, but it is not.
Work is empty without love, so work with love.
Work as if someone you love will use what you make.
Put a little of your spirit into everything you make.
The wind sings to the big tree and to the small grass.
Work is love that other people can see.
Bread made without love tastes bitter and does not fill us.
A song sung without love will not reach people's hearts.
A woman asked about joy and sorrow, and Almustafa answered her kindly.
The cup for your wine was made in a hot oven.
Look deep in your heart when you are happy or sad.
Joy and sorrow always come together, and neither one comes alone.
We hang like scales between joy and sorrow.
First build a small shelter in the wild, then a house.
Your house is like a bigger body for you.
What do you keep in your houses behind closed doors?
Comfort comes as a guest, but later it rules the house.
Your home should be like a mast, not an anchor.
Clothes hide some of your beauty, but not your faults.
The sun and the wind are good for your skin.
Some people say the cold wind made our clothes.
Modesty is like a shield against eyes that are not kind.
The earth loves your bare feet, and the wind loves your hair.
A merchant asked how we should buy and sell, and Almustafa answered.
Trade must be fair and kind, or some people will go hungry.
In the market, be fair when you weigh and count.
Buy songs and music too, because they feed the soul.
Before you leave, make sure no one goes home with empty hands.
A judge asked about crime and punishment, and Almustafa began to answer.
The best part of you is always clean and bright.
A person who does wrong is not a stranger to us.
One leaf turns yellow, and the whole tree knows it.
He knew his words were hard, but he said them gently.
Good and bad threads are woven into the same cloth.
Before you punish, look at the roots of the tree.
He asked the judges some questions that were very hard.
Some people are already sorry for what they did.
Look at everything in the full light before you judge.
A lawyer asked about laws, and Almustafa smiled.
The sea brings more sand, and it laughs with the children.
Some people think life is a rock and the law is a tool.
They stand in the sun but look only at their shadows.
No one can tell a bird not to sing.
A man who gave speeches asked about freedom, and Almustafa answered.
People who always talk about freedom are not yet free.
You are free when you can rise above your worries.
The chains that shine the most can be the strongest.
Fear lives in your own heart, not in other people.
A woman from the temple asked about thinking and feeling, and Almustafa answered her.
He wished to bring peace to their souls, but they must help.
Your mind steers the boat, and your feelings fill the sails.
Thinking alone is a wall, and feeling alone is a wild fire.
Let thinking and feeling help each other every day.
Treat both guests in your house with equal respect.
Sit in the shade and say quietly, God rests in reason.
In a great storm, let your heart say, God moves in passion.
Rest when you think, and move when you feel.
His ship waited in the harbour, and a woman stepped forward.
The woman asked about pain, and Almustafa answered gently.
A seed must break open to see the sun.
Some seasons of the heart are cold, and some are warm.
Some of your pain is like bitter medicine that heals you.
The cup is made of clay, and it comes from a kind hand.
A man asked how to know himself, and Almustafa answered kindly.
A hidden spring in your soul must run to the sea.
Do not try to measure yourself, because you are very deep.
Say, “I have found a truth,” not “I have found the truth.”
The soul opens like a flower with many petals.
A teacher asked about teaching, and Almustafa answered.
A wise teacher leads you to the door of your own mind.
A singer can sing to you, but he cannot give you his ears.
One person's wings cannot be lent to someone else.
Each person must learn alone, and each must find his own way.
A young man asked about friends, and Almustafa smiled.
A good friend can sit with you without speaking.
When a friend goes away, you can see him more clearly.
Real friends do not use each other for gain.
Laugh with your friends, because small joys make hearts fresh.
A scholar asked about talking, and Almustafa answered.
A thought in a cage of words cannot fly.
Some people talk a lot because they are afraid of silence.
Some wise people keep the truth inside and say little.
When you meet a friend, speak from your heart.
A man who studied the stars asked about time.
Yesterday is a memory, and tomorrow is a dream.
Part of you is as old as the stars.
Your love feels endless, and time is endless too.
Let today remember the past and look forward to tomorrow.
An old man asked about good and bad things.
A hungry person will look for food in dark places.
A house that is divided is not a house of thieves.
A tree root takes from the earth, and a tree needs that.
The fruit must give, and the root must take.
Even stumbling words can make a weak tongue stronger.
Even a slow walker is still going forward.
A deer is fast, but a turtle is slow.
Everyone wants to be good, some fast and some slowly.
Good people do not ask the poor hard questions.
A woman from the temple asked about prayer, and Almustafa answered.
Prayer is your heart reaching out into the sky.
When you pray, you meet others who are praying.
I cannot teach you how to pray with words.
God is what we need, and God gives us everything.
A man who lived alone in the hills asked about pleasure.
Young people want fun, and Almustafa was not angry with them.
A man dug in the ground for roots and found gold.
A singing bird cannot hurt the quiet of the night.
A bee takes honey, and the flower gives it gladly.
A poet asked about beauty, and Almustafa began to answer.
Hurt people say that beauty is soft and kind.
Passionate people say that beauty is strong like a storm.
Tired people say that beauty is a soft voice.
The night guards say beauty comes with the dawn.
People in winter say beauty will come with spring.
Beauty is not something we need; it is a joy.
You can see beauty even with closed eyes.
Beauty is like a garden that always has flowers.
Beauty is life with its veil taken off.
The old priest asked about religion, and Almustafa smiled kindly.
You cannot keep one hour for God and another for yourself.
All your hours are like wings that fly across space.
A bird in a cage cannot sing its best song.
Some people open the window for God, and then close it.
Your daily life is your temple, so bring all of yourself.
Take everyone with you when you go to pray.
Look at your children playing, and you will see God.
God can be seen in the clouds and in the rain.
God smiles in the flowers and waves in the trees.
Then Almitra spoke and asked him to tell them about death.
You want to know the secret of death, said Almustafa.
You can only find it by looking in the heart of life.
An owl sees well in the dark but is blind in the day.
Open your heart wide to life, and you will understand death.
Life and death are one, like a river and the sea.
Deep in your hopes, you already know a little about the beyond.
Seeds sleep under the snow and dream of the spring.
A shepherd shakes before the king, but the king means honour.
To die is to stand in the wind and melt in the sun.
When breathing stops, the breath is free to rise and look for God.
Only after you drink from the river of silence will you sing.
When you reach the mountain top, then you will begin to climb.
Evening came, and Almitra thanked him for the day.
Almustafa walked down to the sea, and the people followed.
The wind is calling me, he told the people on the shore.
He promised that one day he would return to them.
He told the sailors that he was ready to sail.
Our dream is over, he said, and now we must part.
The ship sailed into the mist, and Almitra watched it go.
B1B2: The Prophet is a book of poems in prose by Kahlil Gibran, first printed in 1923. It begins with Almustafa, a wise man who has waited twelve years in Orphalese for a ship.
On the seventh day of Ielool, the month of reaping, Almustafa climbed the hill beyond the city wall. There, moving slowly through the soft grey mist, he saw the ship that had come to take him home.
Joy rushed through him like a bird set free, and it flew far out over the water. He closed his eyes and prayed quietly in the silence of his own soul.
As he went down the hill, a deep sadness settled on him. He wondered how he could ever leave this city without a wound in his spirit.
Leaving was not like taking off a coat, he thought; it was like tearing off his own skin. Yet the sea was calling him, and to stay any longer would be to freeze like water turned to ice.
At the foot of the hill, he turned and saw the ship sailing into the harbour. Standing on her bow were the sailors, men from the very island where he had been born.
He said he was ready, and only one more breath of this quiet air remained. Then, like a stream that reaches the ocean, he would become a drop in the endless sea.
As he walked, he saw men and women leaving their fields and vineyards and hurrying toward the city gates. They were calling his name and telling one another that his ship had come.
When he entered the city, all the people came to meet him, crying out together. The elders begged him to stay, for he had been like a noon sun in their twilight.

Outside the temple, a seeress named Almitra stepped forward, the first person in the city who had believed in him. She asked him to share his truth before he sailed, so that their children could keep it forever.
Almitra asked him to speak of love, and a great stillness fell over the people. He raised his head and told them that when love calls, they must follow, even though its roads are hard and steep.

When love's wings wrap around you, give yourself up to them, though a sword hidden in the feathers may wound you. And when love speaks, believe it, even if its voice breaks your dreams as a north wind lays waste a garden.
Love crowns you with joy, he said, and it can also break your heart. It lifts you up to help you grow, and it cuts you back, as a gardener cuts a tree.
Love gathers us like corn, he said, and then it beats us until the outer skin falls away. It grinds us into white flour and works us with its hands until we are soft enough to be shaped.
All these things, he said, love does to you so that you may learn the secrets of your heart. Through that knowledge you become one small piece of the heart of Life.

But if you are afraid and want only love's peace and pleasure, you should leave love's threshing floor. In that world without seasons you will laugh, but not all of your laughter, and weep, but not all of your tears.
Love gives nothing except itself, he said, and it takes nothing except from itself. It does not own anything, and no one can own it, because love is enough for love.
When you love, do not say that God is in your heart, but that you are in the heart of God. And do not think you can steer love, for if it finds you worthy, it will steer you.

Love has no wish except to be fulfilled, he said, and if you must have wishes of your own, let them be these. Melt like a running brook that sings its tune to the night, and bleed gladly from your own tenderness.
Wake at dawn with a winged heart and give thanks for another day of loving, he said. Rest at noon to think about love's joy, return home with gratitude, and sleep with a prayer for the one you love.
Almitra spoke again, and this time she asked him what he could tell them about marriage. Near the front, a young bride and groom held hands tightly and waited to hear his answer.
You were born together, he said, and you will stay together for ever. You will still be together when the white wings of death scatter your days.
Yet let there be some spaces in your togetherness, he went on, and let the winds of heaven dance between you. A closeness with no room in it soon becomes a cage for both of you.
Love one another, he said, but do not turn your love into a rope that ties you. Let it be a moving sea between the two shores of your souls.
Fill each other's cup, he said, but do not drink from only one cup. Give each other some of your bread, but do not eat from the same loaf.
Sing and dance together and be happy, he said, but let each of you be alone as well. The strings of a lute are separate, yet they shake with the same music.
Give your hearts to each other, he said, but do not put them into each other's keeping. Only the hand of Life is big enough to hold your hearts.

Stand together, he said, but do not stand too near to one another, for closeness can become a shadow. The pillars of the temple stand apart, and the oak and the cypress do not grow in each other's shade.
In the crowd, the young bride and groom slowly loosened their hands. They looked at each other and smiled, for they saw that room between them was not distance.
Then a woman with a baby held against her chest pressed through the crowd. The people stepped aside to let her pass, for they could see she had a question.

The woman asked him to speak to them about children, and the crowd leaned forward to listen. He answered that her children were not really hers, but the sons and daughters of Life's own longing for itself.
They come through you, he said, but they do not come from you. Although they live in your home and call you by name, they do not belong to you.
You may give your children your love, he said, but not your thoughts. They already have thoughts of their own, and they will keep them.
You may give their bodies a house, he said, but not their souls. Their souls live in the house of tomorrow, which you cannot visit, not even in your dreams.
You may try to be like your children, he said, but do not try to make them like you. Life does not go backward, and it does not wait with yesterday.
The baby in the woman's arms woke up and took hold of her finger with a tiny hand. Almustafa smiled at the child, and for a moment the whole crowd was quiet and tender.
You are the bows, he said, and your children are living arrows sent out into the world. The Archer, who is greater than all of us, sees the target on the road of the infinite.
The Archer bends you with His great strength, he said, so that His arrows may fly swift and far. It is hard to be bent, but it is for their sake.
Let your bending in the Archer's hand be a joy, he said. For just as He loves the arrow that flies, He loves the bow that stays steady.
In the crowd, a father lifted his small son onto his shoulders. The boy pointed at the ship in the harbour, and everyone near them laughed softly.

The rich man in fine clothes asked him to speak about giving, and the people gathered close to hear. You give very little, Almustafa said, when you give only your possessions, and you truly give when you give yourself.

Think of a careful dog, he said, that buries his bones in the trackless sand as he follows pilgrims to the holy city. And what is fear of need but need itself, since dread of thirst beside a full well is a thirst that never ends?
Some people give a little of the much they have, he said, and a hidden wish for thanks spoils their gifts. Others have little and give it all, because they trust life, and their purse is never empty.

Some give with joy, and that joy is their reward, while others give with pain, and that pain becomes their baptism. But the best givers give like the myrtle, which breathes its sweetness into the valley without thinking of itself.
It is good to give when you are asked, he said, but it is better to give before anyone asks. Give now, so that the season of giving is yours and not your heirs'.

Who are you, he asked the rich man, that people should unveil their pride to prove they deserve your gift? First see that you deserve to be a giver, for it is Life that gives to Life, and you are only a witness.

An old innkeeper asked him about eating and drinking, and Almustafa said he wished that people could live on the fragrance of the earth. But since they must take life in order to eat, let every meal be an act of worship.

Let your table be like an altar, he said, where the gifts of the forest and the plain are offered with respect. They give their lives for something that is purer and more innocent in you, so be worthy of it.

When you eat, he said, remember that the same law which gives you your food will one day give you to something greater. And when you bite into an apple, say in your heart that its seeds will live on in your body.
In autumn, when you gather the grapes, say in your heart that you too are a vineyard whose fruit will be gathered. In winter, when you pour the wine, let there be a song in your heart for every cup.
A ploughman with mud on his boots stepped forward and asked him to speak of work. We work, Almustafa said, to keep pace with the earth, for to be idle is to become a stranger to the seasons.
When you work, he said, you are a flute, and the whispering of the hours turns to music in your heart. Which of you would choose to be a silent reed while everything else sings?
You have always been told that work is a curse and labour a misfortune, he said. But when you work, you fulfil a part of the earth's furthest dream, which was given to you when that dream was born.
Life is dark without a wish to move, he said, and every wish is blind without knowledge. Knowledge is useless without work, and work is empty without love, which binds you to yourself and to others.

To work with love is to weave cloth with threads drawn from your heart, as if your beloved were going to wear it. It is to build a house with affection, and to sow seeds with tenderness and gather the harvest with joy.
Fill everything you make with a breath of your own spirit, he said, as a singer fills a song with breath. And know that all the blessed dead stand around you and watch you work with love.
Some of you say that the man who carves marble is nobler than the man who ploughs the soil, he said. But the wind speaks no more sweetly to the great oaks than to the smallest blade of grass.
Work is love made visible, he told them, and all the labour in the world is empty without it. If you can work only with distaste, sit at the temple gate and take gifts from those who work with joy.
If you bake bread without caring, he said, you bake a bitter bread that feeds only half of a person's hunger. And if you grudge the crushing of the grapes, your grudge puts poison into the wine.

Even if you sing like an angel, he said, without love you muffle the voices of the day and the night. In the crowd, a weaver was smiling already, and the baker, who had been listening hard, slowly began to smile too.
A woman with tears still on her cheeks asked him to speak of joy and sorrow. Your joy is your sorrow without its mask, he said, and the well of your laughter was often filled with tears.
The deeper sorrow cuts into you, he said, the more joy you can hold. The cup that holds your wine was burned in the potter's oven, and the wood of your lute was hollowed with knives.
When you are happy, look deep into your heart: what gave you sorrow once is giving you joy now. And when you are sad, look again, and you will see that you weep for what was once your delight.
Some of you say that joy is greater than sorrow, and others say that sorrow is greater. But they are inseparable, and when one sits alone with you at your table, the other is asleep on your bed.
Truly you are hung like scales between your joy and your sorrow, he said. Only when you are empty of both are you perfectly still, and then you are in balance.

A mason with dusty hands stepped forward and asked him to speak of the houses that people build. Build a bower in the wilderness out of your imagination, Almustafa said, before you build a house within the city walls.
Your house is your larger body, he told the mason, and it grows in the warmth of the sun. It sleeps in the stillness of the night, and it dreams of leaving the city for the grove or the hilltop.
What do you have in these houses, people of Orphalese, and what do you guard behind fastened doors? Have you peace, and memories, and beauty that lifts the heart, or have you only comfort?
Comfort enters the house as a guest, he warned, then becomes the host, and in the end it becomes the master. Its hands are as soft as silk, but its heart is made of iron, and it never lets go.
But you are children of space, he said, and you will not be trapped or tamed. Let your house be a mast, not an anchor, and let it guard your life as an eyelid guards the eye.
A weaver, who was wearing a robe of her own making, asked him to speak of clothes. Your clothes hide much of your beauty, he said, but they do not hide what is not beautiful in you.
Would that you could meet the sun and the wind with more of your skin and less of your clothing, he said. For the breath of life is in the sunlight, and the hand of life is in the wind.
Some of you say that the north wind wove the clothes you wear, he said. Yes, it was the north wind, but shame was his loom, and softness of body was his thread.
Do not forget that modesty is a shield against the eyes of the unclean, he said. And when the unclean are no more, modesty would be only a chain and a stain on the mind.

Forget not, he said, that the earth delights to feel your bare feet and the winds long to play with your hair. A child who had been scolded for running barefoot looked hopefully at her mother, and the mother laughed and let her go.

A merchant, whose scales had been busy all morning, asked him to speak of buying and selling. The earth gives you her fruit, Almustafa said, and you will not go without if you know how to fill your hands.
But exchange is not always a good thing, he warned, if it is done without care. Unless it is made in love and kindly justice, it will lead some people to greed and others to hunger.

When you meet in the market place, he said, invite the master spirit of the earth to bless your scales. Do not let idle people who sell only words join your trade; invite them to work with you in the field or at sea.
If singers and dancers and flute players come to the market, he said, buy their gifts as well. What they bring is made of dreams, but it is clothing and food for your soul.

Before you leave the market place, he said, see that no one has gone away with empty hands. The master spirit of the earth will not sleep peacefully on the wind until the needs of the least of you are met.

A judge of the city stepped forward and asked him to speak of crime and punishment. When your spirit wanders away on the wind, Almustafa said, you commit a wrong against others, and so against yourself.
Your higher self is like the ocean, he said, and it stays forever clean. But much in you is not yet fully grown, a sleepwalker in the mist who searches for his own awakening.
You often speak of a wrongdoer as if he were a stranger and an intruder in your world, he said. But the good cannot rise above the highest in you, and the wicked cannot fall below the lowest.
A single leaf turns yellow only with the silent knowledge of the whole tree, he said. In the same way, no one does wrong without the hidden will of all of you.

He knew that his next words would lie heavy on their hearts, so he spoke them slowly and gently. Even those who are wronged, he said, and those who think themselves righteous, are not completely apart from the wrongs of the world.
You cannot separate the just from the unjust, he said; they are woven together like black thread and white. When the black thread breaks, the weaver must look at the whole cloth and examine the loom.
Before you judge someone who has broken a promise, he said, weigh the heart of the other person too. And if you want to cut down the evil tree, look at its roots, where good and bad grow together.
You judges who would be just, what do you say to a man who is honest in his deeds but a thief in his heart? And what do you say to one who deceives and bullies others, yet has himself been wronged?
How will you punish those whose remorse is already greater than their wrong? Remorse is the justice of the very law you serve, and it comes unasked in the night to make people look at themselves.
If you want to understand justice, he said, look at every deed in the fullness of light. Then you will know that the one who stands and the one who has fallen are one man in the twilight.
A lawyer in a black robe stepped forward and asked what Almustafa thought about their laws. You love to make laws, he said, but you love even more to break them, like children playing by the sea.
While you build your towers, he said, the ocean keeps bringing more sand to the shore. And when you destroy them, the ocean laughs with you, because the ocean always laughs with the innocent.
But what of those, he asked, to whom life is not an ocean, but a rock, and the law is a chisel? They use it to carve life into their own likeness, and they cannot bear anything that looks different.
What can I say of them, he asked, except that they stand in the sunlight with their backs to the sun? They see nothing but their own shadows, and they have made those shadows into their laws.
But you who walk facing the sun, he said, what pictures drawn on the ground can hold you? You can quiet the drum and loosen the strings of the harp, but who will tell the morning bird not to sing?
An orator with a fine voice stepped forward and asked him to speak of freedom. I have seen you bow down and worship your own freedom, Almustafa said, as slaves praise the tyrant who hurts them.
My heart bled, he said, for you will be free only when your very desire for freedom has become a harness to you. You must stop speaking of freedom as a goal that you will one day reach.

You are free, he said, not when your days are without cares, but when you rise above the cares that surround your life. To do so, you must break the chains that you fastened around your noon hour when you first began to understand.
What you call freedom is the strongest of your chains, he said, though its links glitter and dazzle the eyes. If you want to dethrone a tyrant, see first that his throne inside you is destroyed.
The care you want to throw away was chosen by you, he said, and the seat of your fear is in your heart. All things move within you as lights and shadows in pairs that cling to each other.

The priestess spoke again and asked him to speak of reason and passion. Your soul is often a battlefield, Almustafa said, where your reason and your judgment fight against your passion and your appetite.
Would that I could be the peacemaker in your soul, he said, and turn your discord into one melody. But how can I do it, unless you yourselves learn to love every part of what you are?
Your reason and your passion, he said, are the rudder and the sails of your soul as it sails the sea. If either one is broken, you can only toss and drift, or stand still in the middle of the sea.
Reason that rules alone, he said, is a force that shuts you in. And passion with no one to guide it is a flame that burns until it destroys itself.

Let your soul lift your reason to the height of your passion, he said, so that it may sing. And let it guide your passion with reason, so that passion is born again each day like the phoenix from its ashes.
Think of your judgment and your appetite, he said, as two guests whom you love in your house. You would not honour one above the other, for if you favour one, you lose the love and trust of both.
When you sit among the hills in the cool shade of the white poplars, sharing the peace of far fields, be still, he said. Then let your heart say in silence that God rests in reason.

But when the storm comes and the mighty wind shakes the forest, let your heart say in awe that God moves in passion. Thunder and lightning proclaim the majesty of the sky, he said, and a great passion proclaims the majesty of the heart.
Since you are a breath in God's sphere and a leaf in God's forest, he said, you too should rest in reason. And when the hour comes to move, you should move with all your passion, and not be afraid.
Out in the harbour, the ship tugged gently at its anchor, with its sails and its rudder in perfect balance. The people turned to look, and then a woman stepped forward to ask about pain.
The woman with the sorrowful face asked him quietly to tell them about pain. Your pain, Almustafa answered, is the breaking of the shell that surrounds your understanding.
As the stone of a fruit must break for its heart to stand in the sun, he said, so you must know pain. There is no other way for the seed to meet the light.

If you could keep your heart in wonder at the daily miracles of life, he said, your pain would seem as wondrous as your joy. You would accept the seasons of your heart as you accept the seasons that pass over your fields.
Much of your pain is chosen by you, he said, though you may not remember choosing it. It is the bitter medicine by which the doctor inside you heals your sick self, so trust him and drink it calmly.

The hand of the physician may be heavy and hard, he said, but it is guided by the tender hand of the Unseen. The cup he brings may burn your lips, but it was made of clay that the Potter wet with His own holy tears.
A man with a thoughtful face stepped forward and asked him to speak of self-knowledge. Your hearts know the secrets of day and night in silence, he said, but your ears thirst to hear that knowledge.
It is good that you want this, he said, for the hidden spring of your soul must rise and run murmuring to the sea. And the treasure of your infinite depths will be shown to your eyes.

But do not weigh your hidden treasure on scales, he warned, or search your depths with a staff or a sounding line. For the self is a sea that has no edges, and no line is long enough to reach its floor.
