Never say that you have found the truth, he said, but rather that you have found a truth. And do not say that you have found the path of the soul, but that you have met the soul walking upon your path.

For the soul walks upon all paths, he said, and no one path can ever be said to belong to it alone. It does not walk along a single line, and it does not grow like a reed; it unfolds itself like a lotus with countless petals.

A teacher with a group of students stepped forward and asked him to speak of teaching. No one can show you anything, Almustafa said, except what already lies half asleep in the dawn of your knowledge.

A teacher who walks in the shadow of the temple among his followers gives his faith and his love, not his wisdom. If he is wise, he does not bring you into the house of his wisdom, but leads you to the door of your own mind.

The astronomer may tell you what he understands about space, he said, but he cannot give you his understanding. The musician may sing to you of the rhythm in all space, but he cannot give you the ear that catches it.

And he who is skilled in numbers can describe the regions of weight and measure, he said, but he cannot take you there. The vision of one man cannot lend its wings to another, and each of us must grow his own.

Each of you stands alone in God's knowledge, he said, and each must be alone in knowing God and understanding the earth. The teacher nodded slowly and lowered his lamp, and his students looked at one another.

A youth with bright eyes and two laughing friends beside him asked him to speak of friendship. Your friend is your needs answered, Almustafa said, a field that you sow with love and reap with thanksgiving.
When your friend speaks his mind, you do not fear your own no, nor do you hold back your yes. And when he is silent, your heart keeps listening to his heart.
When you part from your friend, he said, you do not need to grieve. What you love most in him may seem clearer in his absence, as a mountain looks clearer to the climber from the plain.
Let friendship have no purpose, he said, except the deepening of the spirit. Love that seeks anything but its own deepening is not love but a net cast out, and only the unprofitable is caught.

Let your best be for your friend, he said, and seek him always with hours to live, not hours to kill. Let there be laughter and shared pleasures in your friendship, for in the dew of little things the heart finds its morning.
A scholar with a heavy armful of scrolls asked him to speak of talking. You talk, Almustafa said, when you are no longer at peace with your thoughts, and then sound becomes a pastime.
In much of your talking, he said, thinking is half killed before it has had a chance to grow. A thought is a bird of the open sky, and in a cage of words it can spread its wings but cannot fly.
Some people seek out the talkative because they fear being alone, he said. The silence of aloneness shows them their naked selves, and so they run away from it.
And there are those who have the truth within them, he said, but who do not tell it in words. In the heart of such people the spirit lives in a rhythm of silence, like a slow tide.
When you meet your friend on the road or in the market place, he said, let the spirit in you move your lips. Let the voice within your voice speak to the ear within his ear.
An astronomer who carried a watch and a sundial asked him about time. You wish to measure time, which cannot be measured, Almustafa said, and to make it a stream that you can sit beside and watch.
Yet the timeless part of you knows that life has no beginning and no end, he said. It knows that yesterday is only today's memory, and that tomorrow is only today's dream, not far away.
The part of you that sings and thinks, he said, still lives inside the first moment, which scattered the stars across space. In that moment you were already there, and you have never really left it.
Each of you feels that your power to love has no limit, he said. Yet that love rests at the centre of your being, and so time too, like love, is undivided and has no pace.
If you must measure time in seasons, he said, let each season hold all the other seasons inside it. Let today embrace the past with remembrance and the future with longing.
One of the elders of the city asked him to speak of good and evil. I can speak of the good in you, he said, but not of the evil, for evil is only good tortured by hunger.
When good is hungry, he said, it looks for food even in dark caves. And when it is thirsty, it drinks even from dead and stagnant waters.

You are good when you are one with yourself, he said, but when you are not one with yourself you are not evil. A divided house is not a den of thieves, and a ship without a rudder may wander without sinking.
You are good when you strive to give of yourself, he said. But you are not evil when you seek gain, for then you are only a root clinging to the earth and drinking from her.
To the fruit, giving is a need, he said, just as receiving is a need to the root. Each is good in its own place, and neither can live without the other.
You are good when you speak wide awake, he said, but not evil when your tongue staggers while you sleep. Even stumbling speech can strengthen a weak tongue, as a child learns to walk by falling.

You are good when you walk with bold steps toward your goal, he said, but you are not evil when you limp. Even those who limp do not go backward, but you who are strong must never limp in front of the lame and call it kindness.
You are good in countless ways, he said, and you are not evil when you are not good, but only slow and lazy. It is a pity, he added with a smile, that deer cannot teach swiftness to turtles.
In your longing for your giant self lies your goodness, he said, and that longing is in all of you. In some it is a torrent rushing to the sea, and in others a flat stream that lingers in its bends.

He who longs much must not scold the one who longs little for being slow and halting, Almustafa said. For the truly good do not ask the naked where their clothes are, nor ask the homeless what became of their house.
A priestess, who had come straight from her temple, asked him to speak of prayer. You pray in distress and in need, Almustafa said, but I wish you would pray also in the fullness of your joy.
What is prayer, he asked, but the spreading of yourself into the living air? If it comforts you to pour your darkness into space, it is also a delight to pour out the dawning of your heart.
When you pray, he said, you rise up in the air to meet all those who are praying at that same hour. Go to that invisible temple for joy and sweet communion, and not only to ask for things.

I cannot teach you to pray in words, he said, for God hears them only when He Himself speaks them through your lips. But you who are born of the mountains and the forests and the seas can find their prayer in your own heart.

In their silent prayer, they say that God is their winged self, and that it is His will in them that wills. They cannot ask Him for anything, for He is their need itself, and in giving more of Himself He gives them all.

A hermit, who came down from the hills to the city only once a year, asked him to speak of pleasure. Pleasure is a freedom-song, Almustafa said, but it is not freedom, and it is the blossom of desire, but not its fruit.

Sing the freedom-song of pleasure with a full heart, he said, but do not lose your hearts in the singing. I would not scold the young who seek pleasure as if it were all, for pleasure has sisters more beautiful than she.

Have you not heard, he asked, of the man who dug in the earth for roots and found a treasure? Some of your elders remember pleasures with regret, but they should remember them with gratitude, as they remember the harvest of a summer.
Some of you are afraid to enjoy anything, he said, in case you hurt the spirit. But does the nightingale offend the stillness of the night, or the firefly the great stars above it?

In the garden, he said, the bee loves to gather honey, and the flower loves to give it. For both of them the giving and the taking of pleasure is a need, so be in your pleasures like the flowers and the bees.
A poet with an open notebook in his hand asked him to speak of beauty. Where will you look for beauty, Almustafa asked, and how will you find her unless she herself is your way and your guide?
People who have been hurt say that beauty is kind and gentle, he said. To them she is like a young mother, half shy of her own glory, who walks quietly among us.
The passionate say the opposite, he said: beauty is a thing of might and dread. Like a tempest, she shakes the earth beneath us and the sky above us.

The tired and the weary say that beauty speaks in soft whispers, like a faint light that trembles in fear of the shadow. The restless say instead that they have heard her shouting among the mountains, with the beating of wings.

At night, the watchmen of the city say that beauty will rise with the dawn from the east. At noon, the workers and travellers say they have seen her leaning over the earth from the windows of the sunset.

In winter, the people who are snow-bound say that she will come with the spring, leaping upon the hills. In the heat of summer, the reapers say they have seen her dancing with the autumn leaves, with snow in her hair.
All of this you have said of beauty, he told them, but in truth you spoke of your own needs, not of her. Beauty is not a need that waits to be filled, but an ecstasy that overflows.
Beauty is not a mouth that is thirsty, he said, or an empty hand stretched out. It is a heart on fire, and an image you can see even when you close your eyes.
It is not the sap within the rough bark, he said, nor a wing joined to a claw. It is a garden that is always in bloom, and a flock of angels that is always in flight.
People of Orphalese, he said, beauty is life when life unveils her holy face. But you are life, and you are the veil; and beauty is eternity gazing into a mirror, and you are the mirror.
An old priest in a white robe asked him to speak of religion. Almustafa smiled and asked whether he had spoken of anything else all that day.
Who can separate his faith from his actions, he asked, or his belief from his daily work? Who can spread his hours out before him and say this part is for God and that part is for me?
All your hours are wings, he said, beating through space from self to self. Whoever wears his goodness only as his best coat would be better off naked, because wind and sun will never harm his skin.
He who measures his conduct only by rules locks his songbird in a cage, he said. The freest song never comes through bars and wires, and a life ruled only by fear sings very small.
Some people treat worship as a window, he said, to be opened at certain hours and shut at others. Such a person has not yet visited the house of his soul, whose windows stand open from dawn to dawn.
Your daily life is your temple and your religion, he told the old priest, and no other roof is needed. Whenever you enter it, take with you your all: the plough, the forge, the mallet and the lute.

In your dreaming, he said, you cannot rise above what you have done, or fall below what you have failed to do. And take all people with you, for you cannot fly higher than their hopes or bow lower than their despair.
If you want to know God, do not try to solve riddles, he said. Look around you instead, and you will see Him playing with your children.
Look up into space, he said, and you will see Him walking in the cloud. You will see Him stretching out His arms in the lightning and coming down in the rain.
You will see Him smiling in the flowers, he said, and then rising up and waving His hands in the trees. The old priest bowed his head and looked at the world around him as if for the first time.
The day was nearly over when Almitra, the seeress who had first believed in him, spoke again. She said that the people now wished to ask him about death.
Almustafa looked at her gently, and a long stillness fell over the whole crowd. You would know the secret of death, he said, as people of every age have wished to know it.
But how will you find it, he asked, unless you look for it in the heart of life? It is not hidden somewhere far away, but in the middle of everything that lives.
The owl, whose eyes are made for the night, is blind in the light of day. So it can never explain the mystery of light to those who ask about it.
If you truly wish to see the spirit of death, he said, open your heart wide to the body of life. Only then will death stop being a stranger who waits for you at the end of the road.
Life and death are really one, he told them, in the same way that the river and the sea are one. A river does not end when it reaches the sea, but only becomes wider and deeper.
In the depth of your hopes and desires, he said, lies your silent knowledge of the world beyond. You may not be able to say what you know, but you carry it with you every day.
Your heart dreams of spring, he said, like seeds that sleep under the snow. Trust those dreams, for the gate to eternity is hidden in them.
Your fear of death is like the trembling of a shepherd before a king. The king is about to lay a hand on him in honour, yet the shepherd shakes.
What is it to die, he asked, but to stand naked in the wind? And what is it to be touched by the warm light, but to melt into the sun like frost on a morning field?
And what is it to stop breathing, he asked, but to free the breath from its restless tides? Then it can rise and spread, and seek God without any weight to carry.
Only when you drink from the river of silence, he said, will you truly sing. Until then your songs are only practice for the song that is waiting.
And when you have reached the mountain top, he said, then you shall begin to climb. And when the earth claims your body, then you shall truly dance.

Evening had fallen over the temple and the great square, and the first lamps were lit. Almitra blessed the day, the place and the spirit that had spoken, and Almustafa wondered whether he had also been a listener.
Then Almustafa went down the steps of the temple, and all the people followed him through the streets. At the harbour he stepped aboard his ship and stood on the deck.
The wind bids me go, he called to them from the deck, and I must not stay. We wanderers never begin a day in the place where we ended the one before.
Brief were my days among you, he said, and briefer still were the words I spoke. But if my voice fades in your ears and my love is forgotten, I will come again with a richer heart.
Then he turned to the sailors, the sons of the ancient sea, and said that they had often sailed through his dreams. Now they would sail through his awakening, which was his deeper dream.
Almustafa drew one more breath of that still air and cast one more loving look backward. Their meeting was a dream that was over, he said, but in the twilight of memory they would sing a deeper song.

At his signal the sailors raised the anchor, and the ship sailed east as a great cry rose from the people. Only Almitra stayed silent, watching until the ship vanished in the mist and remembering his promise that another woman would bear him.
