Its hero is Almustafa, a wise and gentle stranger who has lived for twelve years in the city of Orphalese and is honoured there as the chosen and the beloved. All that time he has waited for a ship to carry him home to the island where he was born.

On the seventh day of Ielool, the month of reaping, Almustafa climbed the hill that stood beyond the city walls and turned his eyes toward the sea. Out of the mist, slowly and silently, his ship was coming, as though the waters themselves had decided that the waiting was over. The gates of his heart flew open, and his joy rose from him and flew far out across the water.

As he gazed at the ship, the gates of his heart were flung wide, and his gladness took wing and sped far over the sea. He had waited so many years for this morning that the very happiness of it almost frightened him. Then he closed his eyes and, in the deep silences of his soul, offered a prayer of thanks that no ear but heaven's could hear.

But as he descended the hill, a sadness crept over him, and he asked himself how any man could depart in peace and without sorrow. He knew that he would not leave this city without a wound in the spirit, for the days of pain he had spent within its walls had been long, and the nights of aloneness longer still. Who, he wondered, can ever part from his own pain and his own solitude without feeling some tender regret for them?

Too many fragments of his spirit lay scattered through those streets, and too many children of his longing walked unclothed among the hills, and he could not leave them without an ache. It was not a garment that he cast off that day but a skin that he tore away with his own hands. Yet the sea that calls all things to herself was calling him, and to remain, though the hours burned through the night, would be to freeze and crystallize and be bound in a mould.

When he reached the foot of the hill, he turned again toward the sea and saw his ship drawing near the harbour, with the mariners, the men of his own land, at her prow. His soul cried out to them across the water, calling them the sons of his ancient mother and the riders of the tides. How often, he told them, had they sailed through his dreams, and now they came in his awakening, which was his deeper dream.

Ready he was, he said, and his eagerness stood with sails full set, waiting only for the wind. He would draw one more breath of this still air and cast one last loving look behind him, and then he would stand among the sailors, a seafarer among seafarers. To the vast, sleepless sea, which alone is peace and freedom to the stream, he promised that the river would make one more winding before it came to her, a boundless drop to a boundless ocean.

As he walked, he saw men and women abandoning their fields and vineyards and hastening toward the city gates, and he heard them calling his name from field to field. Must the day of parting, he wondered, also be the day of gathering, and was it true that his evening had become his dawn? And what could he possibly give to the man who had left his plough in the middle of the furrow, or to the man who had stopped the wheel of his winepress?

When he entered the city, the people came out to meet him, and they cried out to him as with one voice. The elders stepped forward and begged him to stay a little longer, for he had been a noontide in their twilight, and his youth had given them dreams to dream. The priests and priestesses added that their love, though silent and veiled until now, cried aloud at last, since love never knows its own depth until the hour of parting.

Out of the sanctuary came Almitra, a seeress, who had been the first to seek him out and believe in him when he had been but a day in their city. She told him that his ship had come and that he must go, yet she begged him to leave them his truth, that it might pass to their children and never perish. He answered the people of Orphalese gently, saying that he could speak of nothing except what was even then moving within their own souls.

Almitra asked him to speak of love, and as he lifted his head to look upon the people, a deep stillness settled over the whole square. Then, in a great voice, he told them that when love beckons they must follow him, though his ways are hard and steep and every step of the climb will test them. No one who answers that call, he suggested, can expect to stay safe, for love has never promised ease to those it summons.

When love's wings enfold you, he said, yield to them, even though the sword hidden among the feathers may wound you deeply. And when love speaks, believe its voice, though it may shatter your dreams as the north wind lays waste a garden in winter. Love does not ask whether you are ready, he added; it asks only whether you will have the courage to answer.

The same love that crowns you, he said, will also crucify you, and the same love that feeds your growth will take its part in your pruning. It climbs to your height and caresses the tenderest branches that quiver in the sun, and then it descends to your roots and shakes them where they cling to the earth. Both the lifting and the shaking, he made clear, belong to one love, and the tree is stronger for each.

Like sheaves of corn, he said, love gathers you to itself, threshes you until you stand naked, and sifts you free of your husks. It grinds you to whiteness and kneads you until you are pliant, and only then does it set you upon its sacred fire. In that fire you become holy bread for God's holy feast, which is the purpose of all the hard labour.

Love does all these things to you, he explained, so that you may come to know the secrets of your own heart. In that knowledge you will become a fragment of the great heart of Life itself, no longer a stranger to its beating. This is the reason for the threshing and the grinding, and it is a better reason than any pain could argue against.

But if, in your fear, you look only for love's peace and love's pleasure, he said, then it is better that you cover your nakedness and walk off love's threshing floor. You will pass into a seasonless world, a place without spring or harvest, where you shall laugh but never with all of your laughter, and weep but never with all of your tears. It is a safe country, he implied, but only a half-lit one, where nothing is ever risked and nothing is fully felt.

Love gives nothing but itself, he told them, and takes nothing except from itself, for it needs no other source. It neither possesses nor consents to be possessed, since love is sufficient unto love and needs no other treasure. Whoever tries to own it will find it slipping through the fingers, and whoever lets it go free may find that it stays.

When you love, he told them, you should not say that God is in your heart, but rather that you are in the heart of God. And never imagine that you can direct the course of love, for love, if it finds you worthy, will direct yours. It is a river that carries the swimmer and does not ask for his advice about the way.

Love has no other desire but to fulfil itself, he said, yet if you love and must still have desires, let these be your desires. Let your wish be to melt and run like a brook that sings its melody to the night, and to know the pain of too much tenderness. Wish to be wounded by your own understanding of love, and then to bleed willingly and even joyfully, as one who has chosen the wound.

Let your day, he said, begin with a winged heart at dawn and a thanksgiving for one more day of loving. Let it pause at the noon hour to meditate upon love's ecstasy, and let it return home at evening with gratitude. And then let sleep come with a prayer for the beloved in your heart and a song of praise upon your lips.

Then Almitra spoke again and asked what he could tell them of marriage, and a murmur of interest passed through the crowd. Near the front, a young bride and groom, who had hurried from their wedding feast to hear him, held each other's hands tightly and waited for his answer. Almustafa looked at them with great kindness, and then, turning to the whole assembly, he began to speak.

Your two lives were born together, he told the couple, and together they will remain for ever and ever. You will still be together when the white wings of death come to scatter your days, and you will be together even in the silent memory of God. Such a bond needs no chain, because it is older than any promise either of you could make.

But let there be spaces in your togetherness, he went on, and let the winds of the heavens dance between you. Two people who stand so close that no light can pass between them, he explained, have forgotten that each of them is also a separate world. Leave the openings in your union, and you will find that the wind which passes through them does not scatter your love but keeps it alive.

Love one another with all your hearts, he said, but never make a bond of your love, for a bond is a thing that holds and chafes. Let your love be rather a moving sea between the shores of your two souls, bringing each of you the other's gifts and carrying away what is no longer needed. The sea does not tie one shore to the other, yet it is the only thing that joins them.

Fill each other's cup with generosity, he said, but do not drink from a single cup, for each of you has a thirst that only you can know. Offer one another your bread, but do not eat from the same loaf, so that each of you remains a guest who is freely welcomed rather than a debtor who is bound. Sharing is a kindness only when each person still has something of his own that he is free to give.

Sing and dance together and be joyful, he said, yet let each of you be alone, as the strings of a lute stand apart though they quiver with the same music. No string could play its note if it were pressed against its neighbour, and no song could be made from strings that were all one string. It is the small distance between the strings, he suggested, that allows a true melody to exist at all.

Give your hearts, he said, but not into each other's keeping, for no husband or wife is large enough to be the guardian of another's heart. Only the hand of Life itself can hold your hearts safely, and it holds them without ever closing its fingers. Trust that hand, he urged, and you will be free to love without the constant fear of losing.

Stand together, he told them, and yet not too near together, for nearness has its own kind of shadow. The pillars of the temple stand apart, and it is precisely because they stand apart that the roof can rest upon them and the whole house can stand. Likewise the oak and the cypress do not grow in each other's shadow, and each is the taller for the sunlight it has kept.

In the crowd, the young bride and groom slowly loosened the hands that had been clenched so tightly, and for a moment each looked at the other as at a stranger worth knowing. Then they smiled, for they had understood that the room he spoke of was not distance but a kind of respect. Their love had not grown any smaller; it had simply been given room in which to breathe and to grow.

While the people were still thinking over his words about marriage, a woman who held a baby against her breast pressed gently through the crowd toward him. The people stepped aside to let her pass, smiling at the sleeping child, whose small fist was closed tightly around a fold of her shawl. She stopped before him and waited, for she had a question of her own, and it was about the little one in her arms.

The woman asked him to speak to them of children, and the crowd leaned forward, for there was hardly a parent there who did not long to hear what he would say. Your children are not your children, he told her, but the sons and daughters of Life's longing for itself. They have been given into your care, yet they were never given into your ownership, and the difference between the two is the whole secret of raising them.

They come through you, he said, but not from you, as light passes through a window without being made by it. Though they are with you now, and though you hear their laughter in every room, they do not belong to you. You are only the road along which they travel for a while, and a road must be glad to let its travellers go.

You may give them your love, he said, but not your thoughts, for they have thoughts of their own. A parent who pours every opinion into a child, as water is poured into a jar, will find that the jar has quietly grown a mind that does not fit the water. Listen to those young thoughts, however strange they sound, because they are the beginning of a person you have not yet met.

You may shelter their bodies, he said, but you cannot shelter their souls, for their souls dwell in the house of tomorrow, which you cannot visit, not even in your dreams. Your own house belongs to yesterday and to today, and its doors open toward the road you have already walked. Theirs has its windows turned toward a morning that you may never fully see, and that is exactly as it should be.

You may strive to be like them, he said, but never seek to make them like you, for life does not go backward and does not linger with yesterday. A child raised as a copy of his parents is a stranger in his own time, wearing the clothes of an age that has already gone. Let the young belong to their own day, and let your pride be in how bravely they meet it.

Just then the baby in the woman's arms woke, blinked at the bright sky, and closed a tiny hand around her finger as though it were the only anchor in the world. Almustafa smiled at the child with a tenderness that moved everyone near him, and the crowd fell silent. In that quiet each parent thought of a small face at home, and each felt a mixture of love and fear that no words could contain.

You are the bows, he said, from which your children are sent forth as living arrows, bright and quick and made for flying. The Archer sees the mark upon the path of the infinite, and He knows a distance that no parent can measure with the eye. Whatever you feel as the string is drawn back, remember that you are being made ready for a flight whose goal is not yours to choose.

With His great strength, he said, the Archer bends you, that His arrows may fly swift and far. It is no small thing for a bow to feel itself bent almost to breaking, and every parent knows the strain of holding back and then letting go. Yet the bending is not cruelty, for it is the only way an arrow ever reaches the distance it was made for.

Let your bending in the Archer's hand be for gladness, he said, for the same One who loves the arrow that flies loves also the bow that is stable. The arrow has its glory in the open sky, but the bow has its own glory in the hand that steadies it. Neither is lessened because the other goes farther, and a parent who understands this can watch a child disappear over the horizon with a quiet joy.

Around the square, parents did what the words had moved them to do: one father lifted his small son onto his shoulders, and the boy pointed with delight at the ship waiting in the harbour. The mother of the baby kissed her child's forehead and bowed her head to Almustafa in silent thanks, then slipped back into the crowd. Near the front, a rich man in fine clothes cleared his throat, for he had a question of his own and could wait no longer to ask it.

The rich man asked him to speak of giving, and Almustafa looked at him without reproach and answered that a person gives very little when he gives of his possessions. It is when you give of yourself, he said, that you truly give, for your possessions are only things you guard because you fear you may need them tomorrow. A purse can be emptied by a thief, but a kindness once given can never be taken away.

Think, he said, of the overprudent dog that buries his bones in the trackless sand as he follows the pilgrims to the holy city, and ask what tomorrow could possibly bring him there. What is the fear of need, he asked, but need itself, a hunger that grows in proportion to the fullness of the larder? Is not the dread of thirst, when your well is full, the very thirst that nothing can quench?

There are those, he said, who give a little of the great deal that they have, and they give it for recognition, so that their hidden desire makes their gifts unwholesome. And there are those who have little and give it all, believers in life and in the bounty of life, whose coffer is never empty. The first kind keeps a ledger of what he has given, while the second has long since forgotten the sum.

Some give with joy, he said, and that joy is their reward, and some give with pain, and that pain is their baptism. But there are those who give without pain, who seek no joy and think of no virtue, and they give as the myrtle in the valley breathes its fragrance into the air. Through the hands of such as these God speaks, and from behind their eyes He smiles upon the earth.

It is well to give when asked, he said, but it is better to give unasked, out of understanding, for the open-handed find more joy in seeking a receiver than in the giving itself. People say that they would give but only to the deserving, and yet the trees in your orchard do not speak so, nor do the flocks in your pasture. They give that they may live, he reminded them, for in the orchard and the pasture, to withhold is to perish.

Who are you, he asked gently, that people should tear open their hearts and unveil their pride so that you may see whether they deserve your gift? See first that you yourself deserve to be a giver, and that you are worthy to be an instrument of giving. For in truth it is Life that gives to Life, while you, who believe yourself a giver, are only a witness.

Then an old man, the keeper of an inn, asked him to speak of eating and drinking. Would that you could live on the fragrance of the earth, Almustafa said, and be fed by the light like a plant that needs only air. But since you must take life in order to eat, and must rob the newborn of its mother's milk to quench your thirst, let it be an act of worship.

Let your table stand as an altar, he said, upon which the pure and innocent creatures of forest and plain are offered up for that which is purer and still more innocent in man. A meal eaten in that spirit is no longer only a hunger satisfied, but a promise to be worthy of what has been given. And the grace you say over it, whether spoken aloud or kept silent, is the smallest and truest part of the feast.

When you crush an apple with your teeth, he said, say to it in your heart that its seeds shall live in your body and its tomorrow shall blossom in your heart. Let its fragrance become your breath, and together you and the apple shall rejoice through all the seasons. It is a small and ordinary meal, but it can be made a conversation between two living things, each of which owes the other its thanks.

And in the autumn, he said, when you gather the grapes, say in your heart that you too are a vineyard, whose fruit shall be gathered and kept like new wine in eternal vessels. In winter, when you draw the wine, let there be a song in your heart for each cup, and let the song hold a remembrance of the autumn days, the vineyard and the winepress. The innkeeper nodded slowly, and the people around him smiled, for they had never thought of a meal as so large a thing.

A ploughman, his boots caked with the mud of the fields, asked him to speak of work, and Almustafa answered that we work to keep pace with the earth and its soul. To be idle, he said, is to become a stranger to the seasons and to step out of life's procession, which marches in majesty and proud submission toward the infinite. The farmer who rises before the sun is not a servant of the field but a partner in its slow music.

When you work, he said, you are a flute through whose heart the whispering of the hours is turned into music. Which of you would wish to be a reed, dumb and silent, while the wind and the river and the birds all sing together in unison? To labour is to join the great chorus of the world, and to hold back from labour is to stand mute at its edge.

You have been told that work is a curse and labour a misfortune, he said, but when you work you fulfil a part of the earth's furthest dream, entrusted to you at its birth. In keeping yourself alive through labour you are in truth loving life, and to love life through labour is to be intimate with life's inmost secret. The weary hands that mend a roof or draw a net are doing something far older and holier than weariness.

Life is indeed darkness, he said, save when there is urge, and all urge is blind save when there is knowledge, and all knowledge is vain save when there is work. And all work is empty, he went on, save when there is love, which is the last of the lights and the one that makes the others shine. When you work with love, you bind yourself to yourself, and to one another, and to God, and no labour is then lost.

To work with love, he explained, is to weave the cloth with threads drawn from your own heart, just as if your beloved were to wear it. It is to build a house with affection, as if your beloved were to dwell in it, and to sow with tenderness and reap with joy, as if your beloved were to eat the fruit. Whoever works so is never lonely at his labour, for the one he loves is present in every stitch, every stone and every furrow.

Fill all the things you fashion, he said, with a breath of your own spirit, so that nothing leaves your hands as a cold and lifeless thing. And know that all the blessed dead are standing about you and watching, the generations who ploughed and wove and built before you and who now rest from their long labour. Whatever you do well, you do in the company of everyone who has ever done honest work with a willing heart.

Often I have heard you say that the sculptor who finds his soul in marble is nobler than the man who ploughs the soil, and the painter nobler than the man who makes sandals. But I say, not in sleep but in the full wakefulness of noon, that the wind speaks no more sweetly to the giant oaks than to the least blade of grass. And he alone is great who turns the voice of the wind into a song made sweeter by his own loving.

Work is love made visible, he said, and the world has no other proof of love that lasts so long. And if you cannot work with love but only with distaste, it is better to leave your work, sit at the temple gate, and take alms from those who work with joy. Joy is the one wage that cannot be counted, he implied, and the poor man who works gladly is richer than the rich man who works in bitterness.

If you bake bread with indifference, he said, you bake a bitter loaf that feeds only half of a man's hunger, for the other half is hungry for the love left out of it. And if you grudge the crushing of the grapes, your grudge will distil a slow poison in the wine. In the crowd a baker with flour on his sleeves lowered his eyes, for he knew very well the taste of his own bitter loaves.

Even if you sing as sweetly as an angel, he said, yet do not love the singing, you will only muffle men's ears to the voices of the day and the night. Those who heard him understood that work was not a matter of what one did but of the heart with which one did it. In the crowd the baker looked at the weaver beside him, who was already smiling, and slowly, as a man who has found a better recipe, he began to smile too.

A woman, who had a handkerchief in one hand and a smile on her lips, asked him to speak of joy and sorrow. Your joy, he told her, is your sorrow unmasked, and the selfsame well from which your laughter rises was oftentimes filled with your tears. How could it be otherwise, he asked, when the heart that can hold the one is the very heart that holds the other?

The deeper that sorrow carves into your being, he said, the more joy you are able to contain. Is not the cup that holds your wine the very cup that was burned in the potter's oven, and is not the lute that soothes your spirit the very wood that was hollowed with knives? Whatever has been hollowed out by pain, he suggested, has thereby been made ready to be filled with gladness.

When you are joyous, he said, look deep into your heart, and you shall find that it is only what once gave you sorrow that is now giving you joy. And when you are sorrowful, look again, and you shall see that you are weeping for what has truly been your delight. Joy and sorrow, he suggested, are not two different roads but two directions along the same long road.

Some of you say that joy is greater than sorrow, and others say that sorrow is the greater, but I tell you that they are inseparable. They come together, and when one of them sits alone with you at your table, remember that the other is asleep upon your bed. Quarrelling over which is the larger is like asking which of two wings is more needed by the bird.

Truly you are suspended like scales between your sorrow and your joy, he said, rising with the one and falling with the other. Only when you are empty of both are you at a standstill, and only then are you perfectly balanced. But when the treasure-keeper lifts you to weigh his gold and his silver, he added, then your joy or your sorrow must rise or fall.

A mason, whose hands were grey with quarry dust, asked him to speak of houses, and Almustafa told him to build a bower in the wilderness before building a house within the city walls. For just as you have your homecomings in the twilight, he said, so has the wanderer in you, the one who is ever distant and alone. A house that has forgotten the wanderer will always feel a little too small for the whole of you.

Your house, he said, is your larger body, growing in the sun and sleeping in the stillness of the night, and it is not dreamless. Does not your house dream, he asked, and, dreaming, leave the noisy city for the grove or the hilltop? He wished that he could gather their houses in his hand and scatter them like seed in forest and meadow, so that the valleys might be their streets.

And tell me, people of Orphalese, what have you in these houses, and what is it that you guard with fastened doors? Have you peace, the quiet strength that reveals your power, and have you memories, the shining arches that span the summits of the mind? Have you beauty, which leads the heart from things of wood and stone to the holy mountain, or have you only comfort, and the lust for comfort?

Comfort, he warned, is a stealthy thing that enters the house as a guest, becomes a host, and then becomes a master, taming your larger desires with hook and whip until they are only puppets. Though its hands are silken, its heart is iron, and it lulls you to sleep only to stand beside your bed and jeer at the dignity of the flesh. Truly the lust for comfort kills the passion of the soul and then walks grinning in the funeral.

But you, children of space, he said, you who are restless even in rest, shall not be trapped or tamed. Your house shall be not an anchor but a mast, not a shining film that covers a wound but an eyelid that guards the eye. For what is boundless in you dwells in the mansion of the sky, whose door is the morning mist and whose windows are the songs and silences of night.

A weaver, proud in a robe of her own making, asked him to speak of clothes, and Almustafa answered that clothes conceal much of our beauty and yet hide nothing of the unbeautiful. And though we seek in garments the freedom of privacy, he said, we may find in them a harness and a chain. What is meant to be a shelter, he suggested, can too easily become a small and comfortable cage.

He wished that they could meet the sun and the wind with more skin and less raiment, for the breath of life is in the sunlight and the hand of life is in the wind. Those who wrap themselves from morning to night in layers, he said, may forget that they were ever touched by warmth or caressed by the air. The world is a gentle giver, and we lose much when we offer too little of ourselves to receive its gifts.

Some of you say that it is the north wind who has woven the clothes you wear, he told them, and I say yes, it was the north wind. But shame was his loom, and the softening of the sinews was his thread, and when his work was finished he laughed in the forest. Do not blame the cold alone for what we hide, he seemed to say; much of it we hide out of fear.

Forget not that modesty is a shield against the eye of the unclean, he said, and a shield is honourable for as long as there is an arrow to turn aside. But when the unclean shall be no more, what would modesty be but a fetter and a fouling of the mind? In the end it is the heart that makes a garment clean or unclean, and never the cloth that it is made of.

And forget not, he said, that the earth delights to feel your bare feet, and that the winds long to play with your hair. At these words a child, who had been scolded that morning for running barefoot, looked up at her mother in hope, and the mother, after a long moment, laughed and let her go. Out across the grass she ran with the wind in her hair and the whole warm earth under her feet, and it seemed that the hill itself was glad.

A merchant who had left his stall in the market place to hear him asked him to speak of buying and selling. To you the earth yields her fruit, Almustafa answered, and you shall not want if you only know how to fill your hands. It is in exchanging the gifts of the earth, he said, that you will find abundance and be satisfied, for no one man can grow everything he needs.

Yet unless the exchange be made in love and in kindly justice, he warned, it will lead some to greed and others to hunger. A market in which one man grows fat on another man's need is a poor market, however large its profits. Fair dealing, by contrast, leaves both the buyer and the seller richer than they came, and richer in more than coin.

When you meet in the market place, he said, you toilers of the sea and the fields and the vineyards, call on the master spirit of the earth to come into your midst. Let that spirit bless the scales that weigh value against value, and let no barren-handed man take part in your dealings, who would sell his words for your labour. Tell such men to come with you to the field, or to go with your brothers to the sea and cast a net, for both will be as bountiful to them as to you.

And if there come the singers and the dancers and the flute players, he said, buy of their gifts also, for they too are gatherers of fruit and frankincense. What they bring, though it is fashioned of dreams, is both raiment and food for your soul, and often the best of it. A market that feeds only the body, he added, has fed only half of the people in it.

And before you leave the market place, he said, see that no one has gone his way with empty hands. For the master spirit of the earth shall not sleep peacefully upon the wind until the needs of the least among you are satisfied. The merchant stood a long while with his hands upon his scales, and when he walked home that evening he carried less in his purse and a good deal more in his heart.

One of the judges of the city, an old man in a long grey robe, stepped forward and asked him to speak of crime and punishment, and the crowd grew still. It is when your spirit goes wandering upon the wind, Almustafa said, that you, alone and unguarded, commit a wrong against others and therefore against yourself. And for that wrong you must knock and wait a while, unheeded, at the gate of the blessed.

Your god-self, he said, is like the ocean, for it remains for ever undefiled, and like the sun, for it knows nothing of the ways of the mole or the holes of the serpent. But your god-self does not dwell alone, for much in you is still man, and much is not yet man, but a shapeless sleeper walking in the mist, searching for its own awakening. It is of the man in you that I would now speak, he told them, for it is he who knows crime and the punishment of crime.

Often have I heard you speak of one who does wrong as though he were not one of you but a stranger and an intruder upon your world. But just as the holy cannot rise higher than the highest in each of you, so the wicked and the weak cannot fall lower than the lowest in you. The wrongdoer is not a different kind of creature, Almustafa said, but only the part of ourselves that we hope never to meet.

A single leaf turns yellow, he said, only with the silent knowledge of the whole tree, and so the wrongdoer cannot do wrong without the hidden will of you all. Like a procession you walk together toward your god-self, for you are both the way and the wayfarers. And when one of you falls, he falls for those behind him, as a warning against the stumbling stone, and for those ahead, who did not remove it.

And this too, though it lies heavy on your hearts: the wronged are not always blameless, and the righteous are never wholly innocent of the deeds of the wicked. Often enough the guilty man is the victim of the one he injured, and still more often the condemned man is carrying the burden for the guiltless and the unblamed. In such a world, he suggested, no one can simply wash his hands of the wrongs that other people commit.

You cannot separate the just from the unjust, nor the good from the wicked, he said, for they stand together before the sun like black and white threads woven into one cloth. And when the black thread breaks, the weaver does not blame that thread alone; he looks into the whole cloth, and he examines the loom also. Every flaw in the fabric, he implied, is partly a question about the hands and the loom that made it.

Whoever would judge the faithless, he said, let him weigh the heart of the one betrayed as well, and let him who would lash an offender look first into the spirit of the offended. And if any of you would punish in the name of righteousness and lay the axe to the evil tree, let him look to its roots. He will find that the roots of the good and the bad, the fruitful and the fruitless, are all entwined together in the silent heart of the earth.

And you judges who would be just, he asked, what judgment will you pronounce upon one who is honest in the flesh yet a thief in spirit? What penalty will you lay upon one who has hurt another in body yet is himself wounded in spirit? And how will you prosecute the man who deceives and oppresses, yet who is also aggrieved and outraged?

And how, he asked, will you punish those whose remorse is already far greater than any misdeed they have committed? Remorse, he said, is the justice administered by the very law you serve; you cannot lay it upon the innocent, and you cannot lift it from the heart of the guilty. Unbidden, it calls in the dark hours of the night, so that men may wake and gaze honestly upon themselves.

How can you understand justice, he asked, unless you look upon all deeds in the fullness of light? Only then shall you know that the erect and the fallen are but one man standing in the twilight between the night of his lesser self and the day of his god-self. And the cornerstone of the temple, he added, is no higher than the lowest stone in its foundation, while the old judge bowed his head and sat down without a word.

A lawyer in a black robe asked him what he thought of their laws, and Almustafa smiled as at an old and familiar game. You delight in laying down laws, he said, yet more in breaking them, like children by the ocean who build sand towers patiently and then knock them down with laughter. The whole city, he implied, is a beach on which the same game is played.

And while you build your sand towers, he said, the ocean brings more sand to the shore, patient and generous as a mother with a game she will never tire of. When you destroy them, the ocean laughs with you, for the great ocean laughs always with the innocent and the playful. A law that is made and unmade in that spirit does no harm to anyone, he added; it is only play on the edge of something greater.

But what of those, he asked, to whom life is a rock and the law a chisel with which they would carve it in their own likeness? What shall we say of the lame man who hates dancers, or of the ox who loves his yoke and considers the elk and deer of the forest to be stray and vagrant things? And what of the old serpent that cannot shed his skin and calls all others naked and shameless?

What can I say of them, he asked, except that they too stand in the sunlight, but with their backs to the sun? They see only their own shadows, and for them the shadows are the laws that govern the world. And what is it to obey such laws, he went on, but to stoop down and trace one's own shadow upon the earth, again and again, without ever turning round to see what casts it?

But you who walk facing the sun, he said, what images drawn upon the earth can hold you, and you who travel with the wind, what weathervane shall direct your course? What law could bind you if you break your own yoke without striking it upon any man's prison door? People of Orphalese, you can muffle the drum, and you can loosen the strings of the lyre, but who shall command the skylark not to sing?

An orator, a man whose fine voice was known throughout the city, asked him to speak of freedom, and Almustafa looked at him with sorrow. At the city gate and by your fireside, he said, I have seen you bow down and worship your own freedom, as slaves praise the tyrant who destroys them. Even in the grove of the temple and in the shadow of the citadel, I have seen the freest among you wear their freedom as a yoke and a handcuff.

My heart bled within me, he said, for you can be free only when even the search for freedom becomes a harness to you, and you cease to speak of it as a goal. A man who is chasing freedom is still running after something that he thinks he does not have. Freedom, he suggested, is not a prize at the end of a road but a way of walking along it.

You shall be free, he said, not when your days are without care or your nights without want and grief, but when these things girdle your life and you rise above them, unbound. And how shall you rise beyond your days and nights unless you break the chains which you, at the dawn of your understanding, fastened around your noon hour? Every old habit of thought that you call your own was once a link that you fastened yourself, he said, and only you can unfasten it.

In truth, he said, that which you call freedom is the strongest of these chains, though its links glitter in the sun and dazzle the eyes. If it is an unjust law that you would abolish, that law was written with your own hand upon your own forehead, and you cannot erase it by burning your law books. And if it is a despot you would dethrone, see first that his throne, which stands within you, is destroyed.

The care you would cast off was chosen by you, he said, and the seat of the fear you would dispel is in your own heart, not in the hand of the one you fear. All things move within you in a constant half embrace, the desired and the dreaded, the cherished and the repugnant, like lights and shadows in pairs that cling together. And when the shadow fades and is no more, the light that lingers becomes a shadow to another light, so that your freedom, when it loses its fetters, becomes itself the fetter of a greater freedom.

The priestess spoke again, and this time she asked him to speak of reason and passion, the two powers that seem to divide every human heart. Your soul is oftentimes a battlefield, Almustafa answered, upon which your reason and your judgment wage war against your passion and your appetite. Many of you, he added, go through life like soldiers who have forgotten that both of the warring armies are your own.

Would that I could be the peacemaker in your soul, he said, that I might turn the discord and rivalry of your elements into oneness and melody. But how shall I, unless you yourselves are also the peacemakers, nay, the lovers of all your elements? Peace cannot be handed to a heart from outside, any more than a song can be handed to a singer who will not open his mouth.

Your reason and your passion, he said, are the rudder and the sails of your seafaring soul, and a ship needs both to arrive anywhere. If either the sails or the rudder be broken, you can only toss and drift, or else be held at a standstill in mid-seas. Almustafa himself, who was about to put to sea, spoke of it with the authority of one who had watched many voyages begin.

For reason, ruling alone, he said, is a force that confines, and passion, unattended, is a flame that burns to its own destruction. A mind without feeling builds walls and calls them wisdom, while a heart without thought builds bonfires and wonders why it is cold when the ashes settle. Neither one alone is the whole of you, he said, and neither was ever meant to rule the other.

Let your soul exalt your reason to the height of passion, he said, so that it may sing, and let reason direct your passion, so that it may rise each day like the phoenix from its ashes. Reason without fire is a cold lamp, and fire without a lamp is only a danger in the dark, but together they make a light by which a person can walk. The wise soul, he said, keeps both of these lights burning, and lets neither of them go out.

I would have you consider your judgment and your appetite, he said, even as you would two loved guests in your house. Surely you would not honour one guest above the other, for he who is more mindful of one loses the love and the faith of both. The host who gives all the best food to the clever guest and none to the hungry one will soon find that his table is silent.

Among the hills, he said, when you sit in the cool shade of the white poplars, sharing the serenity of distant fields and meadows, let your heart say in silence that God rests in reason. In such an hour the mind is a still pool in which the sky is seen without a ripple, and order is not the enemy of the heart but its quietest home. He asked them to carry that stillness with them whenever thinking was needed, as a traveller carries a cup of cool water.

And when the storm comes, he said, and thunder and lightning proclaim the majesty of the sky, let your heart say in awe that God moves in passion. There are hours when a person must be carried by a power greater than any plan, and to be carried so is not a failure of reason but a sign that the soul is alive. Such moments, he said, ought to be met with wonder, and the one who meets them so has not lost his reason.

And since you are a breath in God's sphere, he said, and a leaf in God's forest, you too should rest in reason and move in passion. A leaf is still when the air is still and dances when the wind arrives, and nobody calls it unfaithful to its nature for doing either. The soul that has learned both rest and movement is neither a slave to its own storms nor a prisoner of its own quiet.

Far below, in the harbour, his ship tugged gently at its anchor, her sails and her rudder in perfect balance, as if she had been listening to every word. The people turned to look at her, and for a moment the whole city seemed to hold its breath. Then a woman stepped out of the crowd, her face marked by some long sorrow, and waited quietly to ask her question.

The woman with the sorrowful face asked him quietly to tell them of pain, and Almustafa looked at her as a physician looks at one he longs to help. Your pain, he answered gently, is nothing less than the breaking of the shell that encloses your understanding. It is the hard casing of what you thought you knew, cracking at last so that something larger can come out.

Even as the stone of the fruit must break so that its heart may stand in the sun, he said, so must you know pain. The seed does not weep for the shell it has left behind, but only turns its small green head toward the light. And the shell, which seemed in its hardness to be the whole of the seed, turns out to have been only the first of its protectors.

And could you keep your heart in wonder at the daily miracles of your life, he said, your pain would seem no less wondrous than your joy. You would accept the seasons of your heart even as you have always accepted the seasons that pass over your fields, and you would watch with serenity through the winters of your grief. No farmer curses the snow for covering his ground, for he knows that under it the earth is only resting.

Much of your pain is self-chosen, he said, and it is the bitter potion by which the physician within you heals your sick self. Therefore trust the physician and drink his remedy in silence and tranquillity, for the wisest patient is the one who does not quarrel with the cup. A medicine is not judged by its taste, and the patient who spits it out because it is bitter has only prolonged the illness.

For his hand, though heavy and hard, he said, is guided by the tender hand of the Unseen. And the cup he brings, though it burn your lips, has been fashioned of the clay which the Potter has moistened with His own sacred tears. The woman who had asked bowed her head, and those near her saw that the lines of grief in her face were softening like a field after rain.

A man with a thoughtful face stepped forward and asked him to speak of self-knowledge, and Almustafa told the people that their hearts know in silence the secrets of the days and the nights. But your ears thirst for the sound of your heart's knowledge, he said, and you would know in words what you have always known in thought. You would touch with your fingers the naked body of your dreams, he went on, and it is well that you should.

It is well that you should, he said, for the hidden wellspring of your soul must rise and run murmuring to the sea, and its treasure will be revealed to your eyes. Nothing in you is meant to stay buried for ever, because what lies deepest is exactly what wishes most to be seen. The only question, he suggested, is whether you will have the patience to let it come at its own pace.

But let there be no scales to weigh your unknown treasure, he warned, and seek not the depths of your knowledge with a staff or a sounding line. For the self is a sea, boundless and measureless, and it will not be mapped like a pond by a man who walks around its edge with a rope. It is better, he said, to swim in it than to measure it, and better still to learn to float.

Say not, I have found the truth, he told them, but rather, I have found a truth, for no single person can hold the whole of it in his two hands. Say not, I have found the path of the soul, but say rather that you have met the soul walking upon your path. The difference may look slight, he said, but it separates the man who has stopped from the man who is still travelling.

For the soul walks upon all paths, he said, and it does not walk upon a line, neither does it grow like a reed. The soul unfolds itself like a lotus of countless petals, each petal opening in its own good time. The man who had asked sat down on the temple steps and looked quietly at his own hands, and felt no wish to measure what he saw.

A teacher, followed by a small group of students who carried his books and his lamp, stepped forward and asked him to speak of teaching. No man can reveal to you anything, Almustafa answered, except what already lies half asleep in the dawning of your knowledge. A student is not an empty jar to be filled, he implied, but a seed that needs only the right light to wake.

The teacher who walks in the shadow of the temple among his followers gives not of his wisdom, he said, but rather of his faith and his lovingness. If he is indeed wise, he does not bid you enter the house of his wisdom, but leads you to the threshold of your own mind. The best that any teacher can do, he added, is to open a door and then step quietly aside.

The astronomer may speak to you of his understanding of space, he said, but he cannot give you that understanding. The musician may sing to you of the rhythm that is in all space, but he cannot give you the ear that arrests the rhythm, nor the voice that echoes it. Knowledge that is passed from hand to hand arrives only as information, while insight must always be grown by the one who owns it.

And he who is versed in the science of numbers can tell of the regions of weight and measure, he said, but he cannot conduct you thither. For the vision of one man, he said, lends not its wings to another man, however much the two may love each other. Every pupil must learn to fly by his own flapping, however long and patiently the master waits on the ledge.

Even as each of you stands alone in God's knowledge, he said, so must each of you be alone in his knowledge of God and his understanding of the earth. The teacher nodded slowly and lowered his lamp, and for a moment he seemed less like a master than like a fellow traveller who has been told the road is long. His students looked at one another, wondering, perhaps, which of them would be the first to find the door.

A youth with bright eyes, who stood among a laughing knot of friends, asked him to speak of friendship, and Almustafa smiled at the whole group. Your friend is your needs answered, he said, your field which you sow with love and reap with thanksgiving. He is also your table and your fireside, for you come to him with your hunger, and you seek him for your peace.

When your friend speaks his mind, he said, you do not fear the no in your own mind, nor do you withhold the yes. And when he is silent, your heart does not cease to listen to his heart, for in friendship all thoughts and desires are born and shared without words, with a joy that is unacclaimed. Two such people can sit for an hour without a word and rise from the bench feeling that a long conversation has taken place.

When you part from your friend, he said, you grieve not, for what you love most in him may be clearer in his absence, as a mountain is clearer to the climber from the plain. Distance, in a true friendship, does not thin the bond but sharpens it, so that the face you have not seen for a year is somehow the more distinct. A friend goes with you, he added, wherever you carry the memory of the good that you saw in him.

And let there be no purpose in friendship, he said, save the deepening of the spirit, which is purpose enough. For love that seeks aught but the disclosure of its own mystery is not love but a net cast forth, and only the unprofitable is caught in it. A friend who comes only for what you can give him has already stopped being a friend, while the one who comes for the sake of the coming will never leave you.

Let your best be for your friend, he said; if he must know the ebb of your tide, let him know its flood also. Seek him never with hours to kill, but always with hours to live, for it is his to fill your need but not your emptiness. And in the sweetness of friendship let there be laughter and the sharing of pleasures, for in the dew of little things the heart finds its morning and is refreshed.

A scholar, his arms full of scrolls, asked him to speak of talking, and Almustafa answered that men talk when they cease to be at peace with their thoughts. When you can no longer dwell in the solitude of your heart, he said, you begin to live in your lips, and sound becomes a diversion and a pastime. Many a long speech, he implied, is only the sound of a mind that has gone out of its own house.

In much of your talking, he said, thinking is half murdered long before it has learned to walk. For thought is a bird of space, which in a cage of words may indeed unfold its wings but cannot fly. The more we cage our thoughts in speech before they are ready, the more they learn the habits of the cage and forget the sky.

There are those among you who seek the talkative through fear of being alone, he said, for the silence of aloneness reveals to their eyes their naked selves, and they would escape. And there are those who talk, and without knowledge or forethought reveal a truth that they themselves do not understand. A chatterer may let fall one wise thing in a thousand, he said, and be the last person in the room to notice it.

And there are those, he said, who have the truth within them, but they tell it not in words. In the bosom of such as these the spirit dwells in rhythmic silence, as the sea keeps its own slow time beneath the noise of the waves. You may sit beside one of them for an hour and come away knowing more than a thousand speeches could have told you.

When you meet your friend on the roadside or in the market place, he said, let the spirit in you move your lips and direct your tongue. Let the voice within your voice speak to the ear of his ear, for his soul will keep the truth of your heart as the taste of wine is remembered when the cup is gone. Then the scholar, who had come with so many scrolls, laid them down on the temple steps and sat beside them in silence.

An astronomer, who carried a watch in one hand and a small sundial in the other, asked him to speak of time. You would measure time, the measureless and the immeasurable, Almustafa answered, and adjust your conduct and even direct the course of your spirit according to hours and seasons. Of time you would make a stream, he added, upon whose bank you could sit at your ease and watch it flow past.

Yet the timeless in you, he said, is aware of life's timelessness, and knows that yesterday is but today's memory and tomorrow is today's dream. The child you were and the old person you will become are both standing in this present hour, if you know how to look. Time is not a road along which you are carried, but a single sky in which all your days are hanging like stars.

That which sings and contemplates in you, he said, is still dwelling within the bounds of that first moment which scattered the stars into space. Everything that has since been born, every grain of sand and every living thing, came out of that moment, and so the beginning of all things lies close beneath your own breast. In this sense, he implied, you are not merely in time but older than any clock that was ever built to measure it.

Who among you does not feel that his power to love is boundless, he asked, and yet who does not feel it dwelling at the very centre of his being? It does not hurry from one loving thought to the next, nor from one loving deed to another, and so it has no pace at all. Is not time even as love is, undivided and paceless, a whole that we slice into hours only so that we can hold it?

But if in your thought you must measure time into seasons, he said, let each season encircle all the other seasons. And let today embrace the past with remembrance and the future with longing, so that no day is ever a stranger to the others. The astronomer slowly closed his watch, put the sundial away, and looked up at the great sky as if for the first time.

One of the elders of the city, a man whose white beard reached his chest, asked him to speak of good and evil. Of the good in you I can speak, Almustafa replied, but not of the evil, for what is evil but good tortured by its own hunger and thirst? It was a strange answer to give, and the people looked at one another to see whether anyone had understood it.

Truly, he said, when good is hungry it seeks food even in dark caves, and when it thirsts it drinks even of dead waters. A starving man who steals bread has not ceased to long for what is good, and the same thirst that sends one traveller to a foul well sends another to a clear spring. It is not the desire that is evil, but the darkness through which it has been forced to travel.

You are good when you are one with yourself, he said, yet when you are not one with yourself you are not evil. For a divided house is not a den of thieves; it is only a house in which the rooms have not yet learned to agree. And a ship without a rudder may wander aimlessly among perilous isles, he said, yet never sink to the bottom.

You are good when you strive to give of yourself, he said, yet you are not evil when you seek gain for yourself. For when you strive for gain you are but a root that clings to the earth and sucks at her breast, and the root does only what a root was made to do. Surely the fruit cannot say to the root, be like me, ripe and full and ever giving of your abundance.

For to the fruit giving is a need, he said, as receiving is a need to the root, and the one is no nobler than the other. The orchard has room for both, and no tree ever bore a single apple without the work of the darkest, lowest and least admired part of itself. Let each of you honour the part of your nature that takes, as well as the part that gives, for you cannot have the one without the other.

You are good when you are fully awake in your speech, he said, yet you are not evil when you sleep while your tongue staggers without purpose. And even stumbling speech may strengthen a weak tongue, as the child who falters in learning to talk is the child who will one day speak. We should be gentle with halting words, for they are often the first steps of a thought that has not yet found its legs.

You are good when you walk firmly toward your goal, he said, yet not evil when you go there limping, for even those who limp go not backward. But you who are strong and swift, see that you do not limp before the lame, deeming it kindness. The kindest help is not to pretend to be weak but to walk beside a friend at his own pace, and with a straight back.

You are good in countless ways, he said, and you are not evil when you are not good; you are only loitering and sluggish. It is a pity that the stags cannot teach swiftness to the turtles, though Almustafa thought that the turtle, in its own way, arrives at many places the stag never sees. No one is condemned to be only what he is today, and no pace is the whole truth about a traveller.

In your longing for your giant self lies your goodness, he said, and that longing is in all of you. In some of you that longing is a torrent rushing with might to the sea, carrying the secrets of the hillsides and the songs of the forest. In others it is a flat stream that loses itself in angles and bends and lingers long before it reaches the shore, yet both are made of the same rain.

Let not him who longs much scold him who longs little for being slow and halting, Almustafa said. For the truly good never ask the naked where their garment is, nor the houseless what has befallen their house. The old elder, who had asked the question, bowed his head and was silent, and some of those who stood near him thought that they saw tears shining in his white beard.

A priestess, still wearing the white linen of her temple, asked him to speak of prayer, and a hush went through the crowd. You pray in your distress and in your need, Almustafa said, and I would that you might pray also in the fullness of your joy and in your days of abundance. A heart that comes to heaven's door only when it is hungry has never visited in the good days, he added, and so it has never learned how warm the welcome is.

What is prayer, he asked, but the expansion of yourself into the living ether, as a bird expands into the sky? And if it is for your comfort to pour your darkness into space, it is also for your delight to pour forth the dawning of your heart. If you cannot help weeping when your soul summons you to prayer, then let her urge you again and yet again, though you weep, until you come laughing.

When you pray, he said, you rise to meet in the air those who are praying at that very hour, and whom, save in prayer, you may not meet. Therefore let your visit to that invisible temple be for ecstasy and sweet communion, and not only for asking. It is enough, he told them gently, that you enter the temple invisible, and nothing more is required of you at the door.

I cannot teach you how to pray in words, he said, for God listens not to your words save when He Himself utters them through your lips. Nor can I teach you the prayer of the seas and the forests, but you who were born of them can find their prayer in your own heart. If you only listen in the stillness of the night, he said, you will hear them saying in silence a prayer that is older than any language.

And this is what you would hear, he said: our God, who art our winged self, it is thy will in us that willeth, and thy desire in us that desireth. We cannot ask thee for anything, for thou knowest our needs before they are born in us; thou art our need, and in giving us more of thyself thou givest us all. The priestess closed her eyes, and her lips moved, and no one near her could tell whether she was repeating the words or only listening to them.

A hermit, who came down from the hills to the city only once a year, asked him to speak of pleasure. Pleasure is a freedom-song, Almustafa answered, but it is not freedom itself, for it is the blossoming of your desires but not their fruit. It is a depth calling unto a height without being either the deep or the high, and it is the caged bird taking wing without being the open sky.

I would have you sing it with fullness of heart, he said, yet I would not have you lose your hearts in the singing. Some of your young people seek pleasure as if it were everything, and they are judged and rebuked, but I would not judge nor rebuke them; I would let them seek. For in their seeking they shall find pleasure and her sisters, seven of them, and the least of these is more beautiful than pleasure herself.

Have you not heard, he asked, of the man who was digging in the earth for roots and found a treasure? And some of your elders remember pleasures with regret, like wrongs committed in drunkenness, but regret is the beclouding of the mind and not its chastisement. They should remember their pleasures with gratitude, as they would the harvest of a summer, though if it comforts them to regret, he added kindly, let them be comforted.

There are also those among you who are neither young enough to seek nor old enough to remember, and in their fear they shun every pleasure, lest they offend the spirit. But who can offend the spirit, he asked: shall the nightingale offend the stillness of the night, or the firefly the stars? Your body is the harp of your soul, he said, and it is yours to bring forth sweet music from it, or confused sounds.

Go to your fields and gardens, he said, and you shall learn that the bee takes pleasure in gathering honey from the flower, and the flower in yielding it to the bee. For to the bee a flower is a fountain of life, and to the flower a bee is a messenger of love, and to both the giving and receiving of pleasure is a need and an ecstasy. People of Orphalese, he said, be in your pleasures like the flowers and the bees, and the hermit smiled for the first time that day.

A poet, who held an open notebook in one hand and a pen in the other, asked him to speak of beauty. Where shall you seek beauty, Almustafa asked, and how shall you find her, unless she herself is your way and your guide? And how shall you speak of her, he went on, unless she is the weaver of your speech?

The aggrieved and the injured say, he told them, that beauty is kind and gentle, and that like a young mother half shy of her own glory she walks among us. To a heart that has known only harshness, a soft voice and a hand that does not strike are beauty enough. They are right in what they feel, he conceded, though they have named only what they most needed.

But the passionate say, nay, beauty is a thing of might and dread, and like the tempest she shakes the earth beneath us and the sky above us. For such people beauty is the lightning that makes the whole night visible for one blinding second. They too are right in what they feel, Almustafa admitted, and their beauty is as true as the other's.

The tired and the weary, he said, say that beauty speaks in soft whisperings, her voice yielding to their silences like a faint light that quivers in fear of the shadow. But the restless say that they have heard her shouting among the mountains, and that with her cries came the sound of hoofs, the beating of wings and the roaring of lions. Each of them had listened with his own ear, and each ear had heard what it was hungry to hear.

At night, he said, the watchmen say that beauty shall rise with the dawn from the east, and at noon the wayfarers say they have seen her leaning from the windows of the sunset. So the man who waits for the day looks for her in the east, while the man who has finished the day finds her in the west. And each of them, he added with a smile, is perfectly sure that he alone knows exactly where she lives.

In winter, say the snow-bound, she shall come leaping upon the hills with the spring, and in summer, say the reapers, she dances with the autumn leaves and wears a drift of snow in her hair. Thus every season sends her to the next, and every heart that is cold longs for her warmth, while every heart that is hot longs for her coolness. Beauty, it seems, is always the guest who has not yet arrived, and the one who has just left.

All these things have you said of beauty, he told them, yet in truth you spoke not of her but of needs unsatisfied. And beauty is not a need but an ecstasy, for a hungry man sees beauty in bread and a lonely man sees it in a face. Beauty herself is what remains when no one is hungry and no one is lonely and everything is simply and entirely enough.

It is not a mouth thirsting, he said, nor an empty hand stretched forth, but rather a heart enflamed and a soul enchanted. It is not the image you would see nor the song you would hear, but an image you see though you close your eyes and a song you hear though you shut your ears. Whoever has once known it, he said, will carry it with him into any dark room for the rest of his life.

It is not the sap within the furrowed bark, he said, nor a wing attached to a claw, but rather a garden for ever in bloom and a flock of angels for ever in flight. Beauty is not a function of use, he suggested, but a flowering that needs no explanation and asks no payment. And the poet, who had stopped writing and was gazing at the sky, saw that no line he had ever set down was as lovely as that one afternoon.

People of Orphalese, he said at last, beauty is life when life unveils her holy face to the one who has the courage to look. But you are life, and you are the veil, and what you have been seeking outside yourselves has been looking out through your own eyes the whole time. Beauty is eternity gazing at itself in a mirror, he said, but you are eternity, and you are the mirror.

An old priest in a white robe, who had stood quietly through every question of the day, asked him at last to speak of religion. Almustafa smiled warmly and asked whether, in all that long afternoon, he had spoken of anything else at all. Is not religion, he said, all deeds and all reflection, and that which is neither, but a wonder and a surprise ever springing in the soul, even while the hands hew stone or tend the loom?

Who can separate his faith from his actions, he asked, or his belief from his everyday occupations, and call them two different things? Who can spread his hours before him and say, this for God and this for myself, this for my soul and this other for my body? A stonecutter near the temple door put down his hammer to listen, and the weaver beside him stopped her shuttle, for they had each divided their day in just that way and had never thought it strange.

All your hours are wings, he said, that beat through space from self to self, and none of them can be set aside for pretending. He who wears his morality as his best garment, to be put on for the eyes of others, were better naked, for the wind and the sun will tear no holes in his skin. A virtue worn for show is a cloak that keeps nothing warm but the pride of the one who wears it.

And he who defines his conduct by ethics alone, he said, imprisons his song-bird in a cage and then wonders why the garden is so quiet. The freest song comes not through bars and wires, and rules have their uses, he granted, as a trellis has its uses for the vine. But a trellis is not a garden, and no one in the history of the world has ever heard a trellis sing.

And he to whom worshipping is a window, he said, to open but also to shut, has not yet visited the house of his soul, whose windows stand open from dawn to dawn. There is no hour in which that house is closed, and no corner of it where the light does not come in. To find it, he suggested, one has only to stop knocking at its door like a stranger and walk in like one who lives there.

Your daily life is your temple and your religion, he said, and whenever you enter into it you should take with you your all. Take the plough and the forge, the mallet and the lute, and every one of the things you have fashioned in necessity or for delight. Nothing that your hands have made is too humble to be carried into that holy place, and nothing that your hands have left unfinished is too poor to be laid on the altar.

For in reverie, he said, you cannot rise higher than your achievements, and you cannot fall lower than your failures. And take with you all men, for in adoration you cannot fly higher than their hopes nor humble yourself lower than their despair. A prayer that leaves anyone behind has not yet gone very far, and a temple that has no room for the poorest man in the city is smaller than it looks.

And if you would know God, he said, do not spend your days as a solver of riddles, for He is not hidden in them. Rather look about you, and you shall see Him playing with your children, in the dust and in the sun. At that moment a small child ran laughing across the temple steps with a handful of flowers, and the old priest, who had been listening so gravely, smiled for the first time and held out his hand.

And look into space, he said, and you shall see Him walking in the cloud, outstretching His arms in the lightning and descending in rain. The same hand that scatters the storm across the mountains lays one cool drop upon the dry tongue of a field. Whoever has once learned to look will find that the sky is never empty, but always full of someone coming near.

At last, he said, you shall see Him smiling in the flowers, then rising and waving His hands in the trees. The old priest bowed his head and, when he lifted it again, he looked at the temple, the harbour, the hills and the faces of the crowd as though he had never seen any of them before. Nothing had changed, and yet everything seemed to have been lit from within, as a window is lit when someone inside has lighted a lamp.

Evening was drawing near when Almitra, the seeress who had been the first in Orphalese to believe in him, stepped forward once more. The crowd was quiet, for the light was fading over the temple, and every heart had understood that the hour of the last question had come. We would ask you now about death, she said, and about the road that every one of us must walk alone.

Almustafa looked at her with great gentleness, and a long stillness settled over the crowd like a cloak laid on tired shoulders. You would know the secret of death, he said, as all people in every age have longed to know it, and as none can learn it from another's lips. He did not hurry, for he knew that this was the question beneath all the others, the one toward which every earlier answer had quietly been leading.

But how shall you find it, he asked, unless you seek it in the heart of life itself? Do not look for it in the grave or in the dark beyond the horizon, for a secret that lives in a house is never found by those who search only the road. Whoever wishes to understand the end must first learn to look, with open and unafraid eyes, at everything that begins, grows and moves.

Think of the owl, he said, whose eyes are bound to the night and are blind in the full light of the day. Such a creature can never unveil the mystery of light, however long it studies the sun from the shadow of its tree. And so it is with those who look at death only from within fear, for they cannot see what the daylight of life would show them.

If you really wish to behold the spirit of death, he said, then open your heart wide unto the very body of life. For life is the larger house in which death keeps one quiet room, and no one can find that room who has refused to walk through the rest of the house. Let your eyes rest on the child, the field and the flowing water, and the stranger will begin to look familiar.

Life and death are one, he said, even as the river and the sea are one, though the two names seem to describe separate worlds. High in the hills the river cannot know where it is going, and yet every bend of its course already belongs to the sea. When it arrives at last, the water that was called a river is not extinguished but merely enlarged, grown vast enough to hold the whole sky.

In the depth of your hopes and desires, he said, lies your silent knowledge of the beyond that lies past the edge of the world you see. You have never been taught it, and you cannot put it into words, yet it moves in you as the tide moves in a sleeping harbour. Listen to the quiet part of yourself that wants without knowing what it wants, for it remembers more than your waking mind has ever been told.

Your hearts dream of spring, he said, as seeds dream beneath the snow, folded small and patient in the dark earth. Trust those dreams, for in them is hidden the gate to eternity, and the gate is not locked against anyone who sleeps and hopes. The snow is not the end of the seed, and the winter is only the long breath that the year takes before it speaks again.

Is not your fear of death, he asked, only the trembling of the shepherd who stands before the king, whose hand is about to be laid upon him in honour? Beneath his trembling the shepherd is surely glad, for he shall wear the mark of the king and be known as one whom the king has touched. Yet he is more aware of his shaking than of his gladness, and so it is with you when the great moment comes close.

What is it to die, he asked, but to stand naked in the wind and to feel every false covering fall away from you? And what is it but to melt into the sun, as the frost melts from a morning field and is not lost, only changed into light and air? He spoke without any sadness, as one speaks of a door that is simply the last one in a long and well-loved house.

And what is it to cease breathing, he asked, but to free the breath from its restless tides, which rose and fell with every hour of your hard days? Now it may rise and expand and seek God freely, without any burden to hold it down or any tide to pull it back. A bird that has been carried a long way on a tired wing does not mourn when at last it is allowed to climb into open sky.

Only when you drink from the river of silence, he said, shall you truly sing, and not before, however sweet your voice has been. All the music you have made until now has been the music of the shore, glad and good, but a little afraid of deep water. When the stillness takes you in, you will find that it was never empty, but full of every song you have not yet been brave enough to begin.

And when you have reached the mountain top, he said, then you shall begin to climb, for every summit you have won is only the foot of a greater height. And when the earth shall claim your limbs, then shall you truly dance, lightly, as you have never danced on any floor of wood or stone. He smiled, and his voice was so tender that many in the crowd forgot to be afraid, if only for a little while.

Evening came, and a deep blue shadow fell across the temple and the great square, where the first lamps were being lit one by one. Almitra stood up and blessed the day, the place and the spirit that had spoken through him, and her voice carried softly over the silent crowd. Almustafa listened to her, and he wondered for a moment whether he had been the speaker only, or whether he had also been a listener all that day.

Then Almustafa went down the steps of the temple, and the whole crowd rose and followed him, a quiet river of people flowing toward the harbour as the lamps glowed along the quay. He did not look back at the city until his feet were on the planks, for he feared that one glance would hold him there. When he had stepped aboard the ship, he stood on the deck and turned at last to face the people he was leaving.

Almustafa raised his voice so that it carried to the farthest edge of the crowd, and even the children at the back could hear every word. The wind bids me go, he said, and though I am as eager as any sailor, I would have stayed one more hour if the hour would have stayed with me. We wanderers, who are always seeking the lonelier way, never begin a day where we have ended another, and no sunrise finds us where the sunset left us.

Brief were my days among you, he said, and briefer still the words I have spoken, and I have given you no more than a handful of what I wished to give. Yet if my voice should fade in your ears and my love vanish from your memory, then I will come again, with a richer heart and lips more yielding to the spirit. Death may hide me and the greater silence may enfold me, but I shall seek your understanding again, and I shall not seek it in vain.

Then he turned to the sailors, the sons of his ancient mother the sea, and told them that they had often sailed through his dreams. Now they would sail through his awakening, which was his deeper dream, and the crossing ahead was the one he had longed for through all the quiet years. He was ready, he said, and his eagerness stood with its sails full set, waiting only for the wind.

He raised one hand in farewell to the people and to the long years he had spent among them, for it was only yesterday, he said, that they had met in a dream. They had sung to him in his aloneness, and out of their longings he had built a tower in the sky, but now their sleep had fled and the dream was over. Yet if they should meet again in the twilight of memory, they would speak together once more, and the song they sang would be a deeper one.

At his signal the sailors weighed anchor and cast the ship loose from its moorings, and they took their way eastward while a cry rose from the people as from a single heart. Only Almitra was silent, gazing after the ship until it vanished into the mist, and the white sails grew smaller and smaller against the grey. When the crowd had gone, she still stood alone upon the sea wall, remembering his promise that after a little while, a moment of rest upon the wind, another woman would bear him.
